items.body:
Written for four Ebow-ed guitars, 'Avaeken' preserves a site-specific piece that O'Malley used to accompany an exhibition by Banks Violette. It's a microtonal symphony dedicated to Alvin Lucier and Kali Malone that's almost physically disorienting - RIYL Eleh, Phill Niblock, Pauline Oliveros et al.

It must be difficult to strike a balance when you're best known for creating some of the heaviest, most chest-pummeling drone music to ever vibrate from a stack of Sun amplifiers. But O'Malley's risen to the challenge; 'Avaeken' is relatively minimal, for him at least, but smacks with an intensity that you don't really see coming until your body starts feeling it. Made using four vibrating strings, he tunes the instruments to create that unsettling beating sound that seems to whirl around the noggin as the resonances interfere with each other. O'Malley wrote the piece following a commission from Belgium's ZWERM electric guitar quartet in 2020, performing it a handful of times before they knuckled down and recorded it in Gent's Muziekcentrum De Bijloke, a medieval hospital that's been fitted out with the proper acoustic treatments. 

And if you've been studying O'Malley's output carefully, you'll already know that he's frequently been spotted alongside Violette, the American artist best known for his huge sculptures and installations. The two have been friends for two decades at this point and have worked together multiple times, so when Violette was describing his show 'Wish You Were Here', an exhibition that tears at the fabric of America's subcultural underground, O'Malley immediately thought about this piece. The link might not be obvious, but O'Malley's use of phase cancellation - when "sound energy is eating itself", in O'Malley's own words - reaps ample rewards here. The effect is unsubtle, penetrating oscillations so disorienting that Violette's themes of societal rot emanate from every skewed tone.

O'Malley presents two takes of the same piece, fixing Violette's striking artwork - of a cracked mirror ball - to the cover. And it's incredible to hear him working as a composer for a change, letting the ZWERM quartet do the heavy lifting. Their expertise helps elevate the piece; it's precise, expertly rendered gear, the kind of thing you need to give your full attention to. Surprisingly, it's also got more in common with those Sunn O))) records than you might expect - play at high volume and you'll know exactly what we mean.
items._cn_summary: 这张专辑为四把Ebow电吉他而作，是O'Malley为Banks Violette展览创作的空间特定作品，由比利时ZWERM四重奏在根特的De Bijloke音乐中心录制。乐曲采用微音程调弦，通过琴弦共振间的相位抵消产生令人眩晕的搏动声响，营造出近乎生理性的错乱感。O'Malley将同一作品呈现为两个版本，封面使用Violette的破碎镜球图像。尽管相对其Sunn O)))时期的作品更为精简，但高音量播放时仍能感受到与重型无人机音乐一脉相承的物理压迫感。作品题献Alvin Lucier与Kali Malone，体现了对当代实验传统的延续。

items.body:
Dreader than dread dub vapors from Ghost Dubs, in a lineage stretching from Dadawah to Burial Mix, Vainqueur to Resilent, Pole to Rod Modelll...​

Toiling in Berlin’s deep seam of abstract dub practice that scrolls back to Rhythm & Sound’s earliest via Pole’s dusty convections and Chain Reaction's fritzed mutations; Ghost Dubs embodies the art of dub as method with a strong haul of dematerialised, sludgy tramplers operating close to the scuzzy heart of Kevin Martin, aka The Bug. Uncompromisingly in-the-zone and dank as a bong, the dozen cuts get right under the skin, up-the-pharynx, with an intoxicatingly sedated and hallucinatory quality that impresses murky, vaporous patterns on the back of blunted eyelids and may possibly raise knees to its slompy skank and imaginary physics. 

Of course, the sound is rooted in the innovative, half century-old traditions of Jamaican dub, as established by King Tubby and Lee “Scratch” Perry, and developed by the likes of Scientist or Mad Professor. But Ghost Dubs picks it up at the point where it diffused into techno and noise during the ‘90s, taking that sound as a jump-off into his microcosm of granular, atomised atmospheric disintegration that nevertheless holds to a steady ballast of scoop-worrying sub-bass tremors. No doubt anyone who’s followed the devolution of this sound outside Jamaica, from NYC illbient to Berlin dub techno, will recognise his hands-on-desk tekkerz ushering the sound into oblique new spaces with a canny sense of proprioception that locates it somewhere in fissure between classic and contemporary soundspheres.

From the caustic attrition of ‘Chemical’, thru the inverted mulch of ‘Dub Lobotomy’, to the sensuous but elephantine trample of ‘Hot Wired’ and tumescent swell of ‘Circles Lines’ ,Ghost Dubs leaves his clammy fingerprint on every cut. Some are primed to bend your Clarks, as with the bilgy step of ‘The Regulator’, and airborne skank of ‘Thin Line’, and the harness-tugging pressure of ‘Dub Battle’, but they’re all held in check with a overarching slowness that gels the 12 tracks as a proper end-to-end listen in the manner of Pole’s early albums with a deeply reliable robustness and temper that stakes it out as arguably canonic tackle.
items._genre: dub / dub techno / experimental / electronic / ambient
items._cn_summary: Ghost Dubs的这张专辑扎根于牙买加dub传统，但将其延伸至柏林抽象电子场景中，融合了techno、noise与illbient的颗粒化声响。十二首曲目以缓慢而沉重的节奏贯穿，致幻般的雾状音层与低频震颤交织，呈现出一种黏稠、失重且带有身体压迫感的听觉体验。制作上延续了Pole、Rhythm & Sound以来的方法，但通过更粗粝的质感和对空间感的独特把握，将dub推入新的领域。整张专辑连贯性极强，既保留经典dub的根基，又具备当代实验电子的锐度，适合从头到尾完整聆听。

items.body:
Tyondai Braxton’s new album, his first full-length release since the recording of his 2022 symphonic work, Telekinesis, reveals itself as unlike what came before and marks the beginning of a new chapter with UK label Erased Tapes. First off, there’s a lot more music here, 70+ minutes of pure electronics and sound design. Plus, it’s divided in a way that’s out-of-step with the longer forms the 47 year-old composer/producer has previously imagined into being. Of the album’s 15 tracks, more than two-thirds are sub-five minutes.

"The album brings together mostly newer works alongside pieces composed across the past decade, some of which appeared previously as standalone releases. To fully represent the scope of this period, Braxton incorporates the Dia / Phonolydian (2022) and Multiplay (2023) singles into Splayed Werks, foregrounding the project’s long-form compositional arc. Along with “Salt Point” and previously unreleased commissioned works such as “4 Zones” (2018) and “K Space” (2021), these pieces were always part of a broader, evolving body of material. Here, they are re-edited as newer versions and remastered by the excellent Matt Colton at Metropolis Studios in London and woven into a continuous narrative. The result is not so much a compilation, but a record that traces its own lineage in real time: a body of work composed across years, now fully realized as a single, cohesive statement.

What the circumstantial facts can’t reveal is the social, in-real-life context of Splayed Werks, an expansive episodic work that plants a musical flag on a turbulent period, and on which darkness and ambiance, rhythm and light, instinct and precision, organic textures and messy playfulness all share space. These Werks take stock of a constantly evolving world, as well as the evolutions experienced by their creator.

It may be a perfect album for 2026, a time when the sonic landscape continues to fervently embrace increasingly radical hybrids, at once club soundsystem-ready, art-installation-leaning, and music-school-mediated. But also, importantly, intuitive and hand-crafted. It’s no stretch to say that Tyondai had a hand in building this world. His two decades-plus-long career has seen him co-found electronic prog-punk heroes Battles (which he’s described as “a laboratory that masqueraded as a band”); performing as a duo with Philip Glass; write numerous electro-acoustic and chamber commissions for celebrated American new-music ensembles such as Bang on a Can All-Stars, Alarm Will Sound, Third Coast Percussion, Brooklyn Rider, and Yarn/Wire; having his “part installation, part band” HIVE project appear at The Guggenheim Museum, Sydney Opera House, and a 3-night residency at Big Ears Festival; and deliver a series of technologically ambitious, at times orchestral works for lauded labels of electronic, experimental and future-music, Warp and Nonesuch Records.

Meanwhile, the world outside has also radicalized. Mechanisms behind the creation, promotion, distribution and broadcast of new experimental music have been violently disrupted, even as audiences for it have grown. In the post-COVID streaming age, juxtapositions like “popular” vs “underground,” and “album” vs “collection” vs “project” have been more in-flux than ever before. The volume and acceptance of previously neglected ambient and contemporary classical sounds has been tempered by a lack of critical context, seeded with algorithmic buffoonery and AI fabrication. Such tensions enlighten not just the make-up of Splayed Werks, full of music recorded between 2018-2025, but its relatively simple sonic-collage forms.

The Splayed shapes and structures have also been influenced by the transformations in Braxton’s personal life. That Tyondai is now a father may not come as a surprise, but the fact that the man who rebelled against his formal music-school education in the late-‘90s, has, in 2022 become a professor of music composition at Princeton University, does. This lifestyle change—a full-time academic gig, escaping the careerist hamster-wheel beholden to commissions and collaborations, a home studio as his own workshop and testing ground, with the desire to finish things and the perspective to not be precious about it—is also key to the album’s sound. Braxton’s time is his own, and his idea of what it means to be an artist in our time has evolved as much as the surroundings. This too is what Splayed Werks is about. It may be a cliché to call each ensuing album by a veteran artist their “most personal,” but it’s no stretch to say this one best reflects who Braxton is in 2026.

As a portfolio, Splayed Werks hews to the menu of a dance music meets minimalist electronic composition, a throughline that stretches from IDM absurdists like Aphex Twin and Autechre, to contemporary immersives like Mica Levi and Laurel Halo. (And, to a lesser degree, to Braxton’s comrades and occasional collaborators, Kieran “Four Tet” Hebden, Jeffrey Cantu-Ledesma and Ben Vida.) It’s a world in which the multitude of dirty rhythms strays far outside club-land’s big rooms—though one can imagine expert mixing hands and a world-class soundsystem transforming the dubwise lo-fi linearity of “Oslo” into a psychedelic wonder, while the interplay between the bass-synth and the constantly deviating shuffle on “UnFS” may qualify as a leftfield banger. And its composed beatless spaces have little to do with current ambient proclivities—the at-once aggressive and ecstatic, panning miniature, “Realistic Water” sounds like power Laraaji.

The spectrum of Braxton’s ideas and directions reveals a voracious mind at play, changing up without overcomplicating the proceedings. Two different pieces called (fittingly) “Multiplay” layer and connect skittering textures in beatwise whimsy, before giving way to a droning dread and organised noise; yet each is adorned with birdcalls to balance the synthetic with the pastoral. “Nimble FX” is also built on hyper-jittery stop-start rhythm lines, and great big cinematic synths. All this music feels fluid, seemingly ready to change in the moment rather than having been dependent on some grand design. Meanwhile, longer, older, more spacious compositions like “4 Zones,’ whose short parts assemble into a narrative-free sound design, and the closing “K Space,” whose chaotic ambiance gives way to what sound like Moog hits, are more grounded, their inclusion shaping Splayed Werks into a multidimensional space, instinctive in how it all fits together."

“Every record I’ve ever finished, I’ve been shocked with what it is. I’ve never known it was finished until it was. Then you get to learn about it retroactively. If I’ve done it right, the finished thing will feel like its own personality, its own being, its own vibe. [Splayed Werks] included.” - Tyondai Braxton

items.body:
Carrier winds the rhythmic tension to breaking point on his 4th self-released 12”, flexing fine-tuned muscle memory and inch-tight production in acres of negative space across a trio of soundsystem phantoms that dance in the long shadow of D&B and broken beat science. Huge tip FFO Autechre, Burial, Photek, T++.

Now three years into a generational run of inspirational plates - including an AOTY ’25 with ‘Rhythm Immortal’ for Modern Love - Carrier’s core sense of discipline and restraint continues to yield peerless reward on ‘Thresholds’. A lifetime’s love of, and immersion in, fwd UK dance musics has prompted him to chase a particular dragon of syncopated swerve and cavernous psychoacoustics to logical, next-level depths diffusing that dread pressure with an adroit, tendon-twitching precision and tactility.

Carrier has been instrumental in reminding ravers what was lost when D&B went stadium and pop-chart scale over the past decades, daring to run against the grain, trust his instincts, to return a sense of mystery and bold experimentalism to what was once a thrilling paradigm. This new trio of cuts eke exquisite nuance from tweaked fundamentals, swivelling 2-step off the bone into smoky hall-of-mirrors reflections of ‘Cure’, and specialising in a razor’s edge, toes-off-the-ground sorcery in a recursive, wraithlike zinger, ‘Scout’ that dips to the sexiest, tongue-tip breakdown, beside the tantric, anticipatory chicanery of ‘Black Channels’ which finishes us off with an all-tension-no-release weapon for the ages.
items._genre: electronic / drum & bass / broken beat / experimental
items._cn_summary: Carrier 在第四张自制12寸中，将节奏张力推至临界点，于大片负空间中展现高度精密的制作与肌肉记忆般的编排。三首作品以声音系统幻影般的形态，在D&B与broken beat的漫长阴影中舞动，延续了他对英国舞曲历史的深层浸淫。开篇曲目在2-step基础上扭转为烟雾缭绕的镜像回响，中段曲目以剃刀边缘般的轻盈感滑入性感细碎的breakdown，末曲则以全然不释放的悬念收束。整体在极简与复杂之间取得平衡，以克制和纪律换取幽邃的听觉纵深，呼应Autechre、Burial、Photek等艺术家的实验脉络，同时保持鲜明的个人辨识度。

items.excerpt: Joining the 4AD roster, NYC avant-rock four piece YHWH Nailgun unload an 11-minute clip of pure math-punk artillery, all demon-possessed vocals, screaming organs, angular riffs and byzantine rhythms. Think U.S. Maple, Battles, Captain Beefheart, Pere Ubu and Still House Plants blended with 'Scum'-era Napalm Death and you'll have some idea. items.body:
Joining the 4AD roster, NYC avant-rock four piece YHWH Nailgun unload an 11-minute clip of pure math-punk artillery, all demon-possessed vocals, screaming organs, angular riffs and byzantine rhythms. Think U.S. Maple, Battles, Captain Beefheart, Pere Ubu and Still House Plants blended with 'Scum'-era Napalm Death and you'll have some idea.

Deployed only moments after Drake dropped not one but three bloated sets of playlist-ready mall pop, 'Magazine' arrives like a cool breeze during a heatwave. See, it's common sense in the AI era to feed the algorithms more, not less, increasing your chances to snag that illusive viral hit by relying on pure volume. Not hampered by the limitations of the format (remember, the "classic album" was only 40-odd minutes because vinyl demanded it), artists and labels have been hedging their bets, packing records with collaborations, remixes and undeveloped ideas in the hope that one of them might end up getting even half the traction of AFX's seemingly throwaway 'QKThr'. YHWH Nailgun laugh in the face of this logic, not just challenging 2026's idea of what an album should be, but 1966's, too. If you thought '45 Pounds' was lean, 'Magazine' trims even more aesthetic fat, cooking down the meat of jazz fusion, prog, noise rock, post-punk and grindcore like it's Wagyu, searing it off and providing just an umami-rich shaving to taste.

The whole process is surprising because so many of YHWH Nailgun's references were already bloated. The prog rock era was when the double album became almost commonplace; 'Magazine' meanwhile could quite easily be crammed onto a 7" at 45RPM. And yet, they've only increased in power since last year. Opener 'Ghost of Love' does more in a minute-and-a-half than most tracks do in three or four times the duration, spinning Jack Tobias' carnivalesque, Farfisa-like synths around Sam Pickard's pliant drums like matted spiderwebs, but leaving just enough room for Zack Borzone's no-wave shouts and Saguiv Rosenstock's hacking fragments of melody. 'Stillness Blues' is shorter still and somehow packs even more in, assembling screamo brickwork over industrial strength bass rasps using Pickard's clattery start-stop patterns as the mortar. It's hard to say this stuff's exhausting - it's over before you've even really come to grips with it - but YHWH Nailgun have a way of drawing you back in, again and again, just to try and catch a whiff of what's actually going on. 

There's the Radiohead-like moan of 'Innocent Sigh', the Eli Keszler-does-Pere Ubu intensity of the minute-long 'Ballerina' and the title track, 35 seconds of breakneck beats, bleeps and shouted phrases that rudely cuts off before it's even had the chance to fully extend its claws. It's a shocker, an eccentric, hyper skillful, deeply original blur of influences and innovation that really does remind us just how punchy rock music can be.
items._genre: avant-rock / math-punk / noise rock / post-punk / grindcore
items._cn_summary: 纽约前卫摇滚四重奏的这张作品，以极短篇幅呈现高密度声响，人声如着魔，管风琴尖叫，吉他线条棱角分明，节奏繁复。专辑刻意对抗流媒体时代以数量取胜的逻辑，将爵士融合、前卫摇滚、噪音摇滚、后朋克与碾核等元素压缩至极限，甚至可放入45转七寸唱片。开篇曲一分半钟内即完成大量信息，后续曲目更短，标题曲仅35秒便戛然而止。乐评认为其兼具冲击力与高度原创性，在极简形式中展现复杂编排。

items.body:
HTRK slickly seduce with the unheimlich sensuality on 'Work (Work, Work)'.

While it may be gauche to attribute the lightless mood of this LP to the departure of Sean Stewart in 2010, it certainly lends some inescapable context. It's hardly like they were doing tween-pop previously, but the sense of gloom and dystopia is almost suffocatingly closer to the edge, from the crawling-on-all-fours pacing, to the detached, androgynous vocals of Jonnine Standish and their perversely detailed production values.

They've got our attention instantly with the sideroom synth eurotica of 'Ice Eyes Eis', and sustain the mood beautifully into the pinging metallic delays and seeping reverb of 'Slo Go', sounding like a Atelecine produced by a young Geoff Barrow after a The Birthday Party binge. Dragging us further down, on 'Eat Yr Heart' the beats become clammier and more echoic, while Jonnine's vox become a ghostly vapour trail of condensed reverb. At the album's apex, 'Skinny', the beats feel like a dystrophied version of something from Mika Vainio's 'Life, It Eats You Up…' album, and 'Synthetik' serves a tangibly textured taste of steely Techno pulses and opiated post-punk guitar drifts into 'Poison'.

To close, the heavy-hearted atmopshere weighs heavier still on 'Work That Body', tracing anaesthetic connections with their Melbourne forefathers, Pelican Daughters, before the bleak romance of 'Love Triangle' and the blank-eyed writhe of 'Body Double'.

For fans of occluded sonics from Pump to Atelecine or Mika Vainio, this is a strongly recommended listen.
items._cn_summary: 这张专辑以阴郁而诡魅的感官性贯穿始终，在成员离队后的背景下更显压抑与反乌托邦气息。整体以匍匐般的缓慢节奏、疏离的中性嗓音和过度细节化的制作构建出近乎令人窒息的暗黑氛围。开篇曲用合成器营造出私密的电子情色质感，随后在金属延迟与弥散混响中，呈现出类似工业声响与后朋克前辈交叠的质感。中段节拍变得潮湿而多回声，人声如同凝结混响的幽灵轨迹；高潮部分被比作芬兰电子乐手米卡·瓦伊尼奥式的萎缩节拍，并加入钢铁质感的电子脉冲与麻醉感的后朋吉他。后半张延续沉重情绪，既勾连墨尔本本地的暗潮脉络，也保持冷冽浪漫与空洞扭动的身体感。整体适合偏好晦暗、遮蔽与高密度声响细节的听者。

items.body:
Swedish jazz icon Christer Bothén returns to Black Truffle backed by Ghosted's Oren Ambarchi, Johan Berthling and Andreas Werliin, playing bass clarinet and donso n’goni over the trio's signature kraut-jazz grooves. Hypnotic, trance-inducing biz FFO Natural Information Society, Don Cherry's 'Organic Music Society', Jon Hassell, The Necks.

If you're up on your Swedish jazz, there's no way you won't have stumbled across multi-instrumentalist Bothén. He's still best known for palling around with Don Cherry when the jazz great moved to Scandinavia, even teaching him how to play the donso n'goni, a sacred "hunter's harp" from the Wassoulou region in West Africa that Bothén had picked up when he was in Mali. And he's continued to perform with various local artists and outfits, conspicuously appearing on Ghosted's 2022 debut album just mere moments before Ambarchi's Black Truffle imprint re-issued his lost Afro-fusion classic album 'Trancedance'. Last year, Bothén finally issued his first solo n'goni album and now he's back on Black Truffle with this fleshed-out collaboration with the Ghosted crew, leading Ambarchi's Leslie-cab guitar drones, Berthling's bass and Werliin's drums.

Berthling and Werliin take the lead at first on the title track, hammering out a rotating groove before Bothén lets rip on bass clarinet. And playing a side role, Ambarchi might have the most important presence, using his signature phased, organ-like tones to provide anchoring drones for Bothén's spirited improvisations. He's even more pivotal on 'Antigorite', playing cascading staccato notes over those Leslie moans and creating an rhythmelodic foil for the other three players' more traditional interplay. But it's when Bothén plays the n'ghoni that the album really hits its stride; on 'Lizardite', those buzzing tones offset Ambarchi's crystalline twangs, filling in for Werliin's imposing basslines. It's the moment where everything else just drops into place, creating a structural crescendo before the album careers into darkness on the brilliantly moody closer 'Chrysotile'.
items._genre: experimental jazz / kraut-jazz / world fusion / drone
items._cn_summary: 这张专辑由瑞典爵士老将Christer Bothén与Ghosted乐队成员合作，以低音单簧管和西非多索恩戈尼琴贯穿于鼓与贝斯构成的旋转律动中。Ambarchi的Leslie音箱吉他嗡鸣为即兴提供锚定，在标题曲和《Antigorite》中形成管风琴般的层次；当Bothén弹起恩戈尼琴时，拨弦声与晶体般的吉他泛音交织，结构逐渐攀升，最终落入阴郁的《Chrysotile》。作品融合了瑞典爵士、西非狩猎竖琴传统与迷幻律动，在重复中营造出催眠般的仪式感，即兴与嗡鸣的互动成为核心聆听体验。

items.body:
Required listening for computer music freaks, 'Synthesized Voices' originally appeared in 1976, collecting innovative composer Charles Dodge's prophetic vocal experiments - recordings of Mark Strand's surrealist poems recreated on Bell Laboratories' uncanny synthetic speech tech. If you're into Anton Bruhin's deranged 'Speech Poems', this'll hit the spot.

You've got to applaud DINTE for the timing of this one. Right now, it's hard to tell what's a real voice and what's been cobbled together using LLM tech, Frankensteined from decades of scraped voiceovers and newsreels. Synthesized voices are stapled to short form content and used to provide an air of humanity to mass-generated robo-slop. And listening to Dodge's set of pioneering studies, it's remarkable how the technology has evolved in such a short period of time. In the early '70s, when Dodge began his investigations, heavily synthesised voices were terrifyingly mechanical, usually used to depict malign forces - just cop any of those vintage Doctor Who episodes that feature Cybermen. What's fascinating is that Dodge seems to understand its crucial limitation; he doesn't attempt to make the voice sound more human (and therefore more tolerable), but mirrors Strand's absurdist logic instead, going beyond the limit of the larynx.

Dodge explains that he labels it computer music because it's the Bell Labs computer setup that analysed and synthesised the voices, but he's quick to say that it's not generative music. Each poem was recorded to tape first then fed into the mainframe, that was then able to recreate the language using a pre-loaded archive of words and phrases. This would have resulted in a dry study, so Dodge tested the limits of the system by reconfiguring the parameters beforehand, shifting the pitch contour, the formants and duration of the syllables to radically diverge from the way we actually speak. The eight-minute 'In Celebration' is a great starting point. Composed in 1975, it seemingly shreds Strand's poem of the same name, in actuality locating its spirit, hanging on the word "you" just like Strand does. Dodge works with speed and pitch radically, twisting the phrases into machine-gunned barrages or disorienting decelerated harmonies. The words are still there - "your lungs prepare themselves for an ashen feeling" is a banger - but they've become hoarse, noisy growls or synthetic cries. 

The four part 'Speech Songs' is lighter, rooted in poems that were intended to invite audiences to respond with laughter, yet there's something even more disturbing about a computerised voice noisily bellowing out the same word, stuttering and getting stuck on throwaway rhymes. Really, Dodge hits his stride with the ambitious 'The Story of Our Lives', an "operatic dialogue for male and female synthetic voices" that we'd love to think Robert Ashley heard. There's a similar commitment to breaking down the formula of theater and opera on display here as Dodge corrupts these mundane utterances, forcing out near-songs and high drama from soap opera-ready domestic situations. With Dodge at the controls, the words shift haphazardly from recognizable to horrifyingly alien for almost no reason whatsoever, adding a sense of danger to what might regularly be daytime telly. It's an astute skewering of American culture that's maybe more relevant now than it ever was.
items._genre: experimental electronic / computer music / avant-garde / vocal music
items._cn_summary: 这张专辑收录了查尔斯·道奇于1976年完成的合成语音实验作品，利用贝尔实验室的计算机系统对马克·斯特兰德的超现实主义诗歌进行声音重构。道奇并未追求让机器语音更接近人声，而是主动调整音高轮廓、共振峰与音节时长，使诗句变成嘶哑的咆哮、失真的合成哭喊或急速连发的音节。作品在机械感与诗意之间建立独特张力，既保留诗歌文本的荒诞逻辑，又彻底突破人类发声器官的物理限制。专辑中的《Speech Songs》以轻松语调包裹不安内核，而长篇作品《The Story of Our Lives》则以男女合成声音的对话形式拆解传统歌剧结构。这些创作早于当下泛滥的AI语音技术数十年，却已触及合成声音在情感表达与叙事可能性上的核心命题，是计算机音乐与声音艺术领域的重要文献。

items.body:
Our Darkness descends upon Dark Entries with a reissue of Anne Clark’s epochal proto-house masterpiece from 1984.

"As a young poet, Clark found herself drawn to London’s emerging punk scene. She became acquainted with Psychic TV affiliate David Harrow, with whom she would collaborate on 1983’s Changing Places and 1984’s Joined Up Writing. “Our Darkness,” off the latter album, was released as a single on Ink Records that same year, and became an underground club hit. It’s a singular piece of music: Clark’s lyrics, delivered with equal parts muscular confidence and unease, speak of urban alienation and heartbreak, while Harrow’s production pummels the listener with hydraulic beats and gloom-laced arpeggios. The song’s spirit would prove influential on both the early Chicago house and Detroit techno scenes, where mechanistic funk and existential despair could catalyse dancefloor mayhem.

This reissue offers three versions of “Our Darkness”: the original 12” remix, the Razormaid mix, and a previously unreleased dub version uncovered by David Harrow. Also included is the extended mix of “Sleeper in Metropolis,” another dancefloor hit of Clark’s, as well as the elegiac “Poem for a Nuclear Romance.”

“Our Darkness” channels timeless longing and contemporary dismay, a classic overdue for a little light shed upon it."
items._cn_summary: Anne Clark 于1984年发行的《Our Darkness》以单曲形式成为地下俱乐部经典，此次Dark Entries厂牌再版收录原版12寸混音、Razormaid混音及David Harrow发掘的未发行混音版，并附上《Sleeper in Metropolis》延长混音与《Poem for a Nuclear Romance》。Clark以兼具力量感与不安的诗歌式演唱，描绘城市疏离与心碎；Harrow的制作以液压般沉重的节拍和阴郁琶音构建出机械化的律动。该曲被视为proto-house的重要样本，其机械化放克与存在主义绝望的融合对早期芝加哥house与底特律techno场景产生直接影响。再版内容完整呈现了作品的多重面向，既保留时代印记，也凸显其跨越俱乐部与实验聆听的独特位置。

items.body:
One of electronic music's most influential recordings, back in circulation.

Most readers of these pages will know the story, but to indulge you with a recap, Gottsching was part of electronic krautrock heroes Ash Ra Tempel and in 1981, off the back of a Klaus Schulze tour, sat down one evening and dropped a continuous piece of music which would uncannily imagine the arc of dance music for a quarter of a century.

Early adopters in the Chicago and Detroit warehouses and mediterranean pleasure palaces must have thrilled to the balanced and continuous surging flow of the hour long piece - even over two sides the mix is perfect for building a club atmosphere and suggesting avenues for mixing, whilst using merely two chords throughout. the minimalism offsets the percussive splendour perfectly - several years later the tune was rediscovered and co-opted into the huge italo house smash Sueno Latino, which cemented its foundation in the burgeoning balearic scene of the time and proceeded through several spells of rapturous revival throughout the nineties, not least when figures like Carl Craig and Basic Channel issued their own radically different reshapes and remakes of the piece.

Very satisfying then to have this Gottsching sanctioned edition, where the game might truly be said to have begun in earnest. As they say on the august walls of the Hardwax emporium - buy or die.
items._cn_summary: 德国音乐家Manuel Göttsching于1981年录制的长篇电子作品，一小时不间断，仅用两个和弦推进。乐评强调它在芝加哥、底特律仓库与地中海俱乐部中被早期舞曲人群接受，并预示了此后二十五年舞曲音乐的走向。作品以极简和声支撑持续流动的节奏脉冲，黑胶双面混音衔接自然，适合营造俱乐部氛围。后来被改编为Italo house名曲Sueno Latino，并被Carl Craig、Basic Channel以不同方式重塑，进一步确立其影响力。此版本由Göttsching本人认可，被视为这一脉络的正式起点。

items.body:
Returning to Jabu's do you have peace? imprint, Bristol-based Ukrainian artist Regina Collage reflects on global and personal instability, infusing her haunted, lo-fi songs with tentative passion. It's gorgeous, fragile and deeply personal pop - somewhere between HTRK, Broadcast and Cukor Bila Smert’.

Hailing from Kharkiv where her parents still live, Collage is acutely aware of the lasting impacts of war - the severed relationships, the daily, ongoing trauma. In Bristol, she's away from the front line, but carries it with her, a feeling of "quiet shame" that grounds her latest album's subtle, minimal arrangements. Because although her voice is at the centre of the album, she rarely raises it to more than a distant whisper, sounding as if she's trapped in a liminal space between realities. On 'It Should Be Something', she drowns her moans in reverb, harmonising with echo trails, bass guitar plucks and languid riffs; it's music that won't come as a complete surprise to anyone familiar with Jabu's output, but Collage's outlook is slower, sadder and more exposed. Sure, she plays fast and loose with effects, but the processes never obscure the album's core emotions - heart-melting feelings we haven't heard rendered quite so perfectly since we locked in with Jonnine's 'Southside Girl'. 

'Horizont' is rooted in a kind of bedroom-recorded post-punk that's so slow and gummed up with noise you'd think it was some STROOM-related archival discovery. On 'Davno', her voice seems to float around a simple, distorted drum machine and ebbing analog synths, molded into casual moans that betray Collage's sobering, vulnerable themes. But she's almost in a different headspace altogether on 'I Hope', curling her words around a Hooky-style staccato bassline and anticipating a beat that never actually comes. Each song sounds as if it's a torn page from her scrapbook, not exactly half-finished, but certainly not polished - and it's this aesthetic that gives the album so much emotional weight. We get to reach into Collage's psyche, hearing her own instability as she wonders about a world that's been thrown into chaos. As she reconciles with the situation, figuring out her life in Bristol at the same time, she constructs a sound that's similarly dualistic - unashamedly displaying its roots in the Ukrainian underground while absorbing ideas from her new home.
items._cn_summary: 这张专辑以极简低保真的声响承载对战争与个人动荡的反思，人声如耳语般漂浮在混响与回声之间，营造出介于现实与虚幻之间的氛围。歌曲结构松散如剪贴簿残页，融合后朋克、模拟合成器与鼓机，在缓慢黏稠的噪音中呈现脆弱而深沉的情感。乌克兰出身与布里斯托生活构成双重文化视角，既扎根于地下音乐传统，又吸收新环境的养分。声音处理虽随意但未掩盖核心情绪，反而增强了暴露感与私密性，让听者直接触及艺术家的心理状态。这种真诚而克制的表达方式，使专辑在同类作品中具有独特的感染力。

items.body:
On Kirk Barley’s definitive solo gem, alternative tunings and a tactile feel for pitching rhythms generate their gentlest and most absorbing work, twinkling amid a microcosm of similar, exploratory productions from Mark Fell & Rian Treanor thru to Aleksi Perälä, Beatrice Dillon, Terry Riley & Jon Hassell.

Building on a decade of work spanning cuts for Brownswood thru to jams with Matthew Herbert and Matt Davies, ‘Arc’ finds Yorkshire-bred artist Barley fully indulge formative passions for microtonal just intonation - as seeded in Terry Riley’s ‘Shri Camel’ - and slippery syncopation to the fullest. Half solo, proper, and half peppered with percussion by regular spar, Matt Davies, it follows his nose for open frontiers of alternative tunings and wonky meter with the blend of low key modesty and prism-pushing tekkerz that have long endeared his work to lovers of lower case experimental music. 

Sweetly balanced between timeless, folk-soul-wise and futurist sensibilities, the half hour suite knits hyaline synths and rippling gamelan metallophonics with clarinet and guitar in lissom, sloshing shapes that effortlessly seduce, rather than demand, the listener’s attention. In particular we are drawn to the bits in duo with Davies, floating sublime ideas in the dreamlike, inverted dub architexture of ‘Ion’, settling on mind like a strangely bucolic Incus work on ’Sundry’, and thru the exquisite, tip-toed rhythms of ‘Ecstatic’, to a trippier, bittersweet type of ante-chamber music on ‘Fret (Hear)’.

He’s also deeply charming when left to his own devices. Ambient opener ‘Billow’ calls to mind the tenderness of Cotton Goods works, and ‘Knead’ chases a certain geist of Irdial or Plaid-esque gamelantronica into the sublime title tune, while ‘Prism’ most beautifully ties all his interests in a melting dream sequence which he caps with the harmonic nightlight glow of ‘Column’.
items._cn_summary: Kirk Barley的《Arc》以另类调弦和微分音纯律为基底，结合不规则的切分节奏，生成柔和而专注的声响。专辑一半为独奏，一半与打击乐手Matt Davies合作，融入清澈合成器、甘美兰金属敲击、单簧管与吉他，形成如水波般流动的形态。受Terry Riley《Shri Camel》启发，同时与Mark Fell、Beatrice Dillon等人的探索一脉相承。曲目如《Ion》《Sundry》展现梦幻倒置的dub质感，《Ecstatic》以精细踮脚般的节奏推进，《Prism》则将其兴趣综合为融化的梦境序列。整体在民谣般的温情与未来主义之间取得平衡，以低姿态但精密的声响设计吸引听众，延续了英国下ercase实验音乐的传统。

items.body:
Not the birth of acid house, but a thrilling piece of synth raga set to brisk disco beats, Bollywood soundtrack composer Charanjit Singh’s ’82 LP is simply a landmark in its own right, and a proper ‘floor-filler to boot.

Since its first reissue in 2010, Singh’s cult, early use of the TB-303 on driving machine beats has been erroneously hailed the birth of acid house. OK the formula is there, but Chris Carter’s ‘Spaces Between’ (1980) and his CTI jam ‘Dancing Ghosts’ got there a couple of years before Singh, at the very least, and neither really inform the genius of Phuture and co a few years later. In any event, ‘Synthesizing: Ten Ragas To A Disco Beat’ is just an incredibly fruity boost to any club, revolving 10 hypnotic, pulsating jams closer to early Irdial (say, Aqua Regia’s ‘Hot Love’) than owt from the Chi. 

Taking a minute away from knocking out Bollywood scores and leading his wedding band covering popular songs, Singh would land upon a stroke of genius with ‘Ten Ragas To A Disco Beat’, finding the sweetspot between prevailing hi-NRG disco and millennia of raga traditions that patently transcended the sum of their parts more than 40 years later. It sounds very much of its time, rather than the stripped back linearity of later acid house, evidenced in the florid keyboard urges of ‘Raga Bhupali’, transposing a steamy sort of club canter to somewhere even more humid.

A real club evergreen, suck it and see.

items._cn_summary: 这张一九八二年的专辑出自宝莱坞配乐作曲家查兰吉特·辛格之手，将印度拉格旋律与高速迪斯科节拍结合，并以早期合成器塑造出循环、脉动的声响。它常被误认为酸性浩室的源头，但乐评指出此前已有更早的类似尝试；不过作为独立作品，它依然是一个里程碑。十首曲目在舞曲动能与千年拉格传统之间找到平衡，键盘装饰让俱乐部节奏带上湿热氛围。其声音带有鲜明时代感，不同于后来酸性浩室的极简线性，却凭借独特的融合成为俱乐部常青曲目。

items.body:
Tighter and tidier than last year's 'Electric Chair', Cities Aviv's latest set is a psilocybin-infused dream sequence packed with fuzzy ambient interludes, loopy clouded reflections and stream-of-consciousness recitations. 

 Gavin Mays has always been on the perimeter of any given scene or other, happy enough to draw his own landscape while everyone else churns up the same mud. And that's truer than ever on his recent run; operating on his lonesome, Mays creates music that can't be pigeonholed - it's barely even rap. He spits on the two-part title track, but his words dilate awkwardly over noisy, new age-esque synths and blown-out, pitch-deformed rhythms. They might not even be strictly on the beat at all, that's not the point - Mays creates a mood that he prolongs throughout 'Even Colder Spring'. The second part of the title track sounds more like Seefeel than it does MF DOOM, anyways.

It's not always easy to digest - we'll admit we struggled with 'Spinnin & Spinnin' - but 'Even Colder Spring' is surprisingly approachable compared with many of his recent releases. And what it lacks in cohesion it more than makes up for in pure eccentricity. "Maybe Mars is bougie," he quips over electric piano arpeggios and feedback squeals on 'Tribeca', before breathing lullabies over slowed-down soul samples on 'Concrete Masks'.
items._genre: experimental hip hop / ambient / electronic / noise
items._cn_summary: 这张专辑延续了Gavin Mays一贯的游离姿态，以迷幻梦境般的氛围段落、模糊的循环反射和意识流念白构成。人声在嘈杂的新时代合成器和失真人声与节奏上扭曲延展，并不严格遵循节拍，整体氛围感优先于说唱技术。第二部分的标题曲更接近Seefeel式的氛围电子而非MF DOOM式的说唱。专辑虽在连贯性上有所欠缺，但以纯粹的怪诞个性弥补，例如《Tribeca》中电钢琴琶音与反馈尖啸间的俏皮念白，《Concrete Masks》中慢速灵魂采样上的摇篮曲式吟唱。适合喜欢实验嘻哈与氛围电子交叉地带的听众。

items.body:
Billed as a sequel to 2024's 'Something in the Room She Moves', 'Materia' augments and extends Julia Holter's unique vision, chopping and screwing the Hildegard von Bingen-inspired title track and swaddling it with more psychotropic chamber pop experiments. Dizzier and more surreal than the original album, it might be even more dazzling - properly vital FFO Mabe Fratti, Jessica Pratt, ANOHNI or Jenny Hval.

Ever since we got snagged by 2011's AOTY 'Tragedy', we've been captivated by her particular fusion of baroque pop, high drama and groggy minimalism - elements that inevitably arrive tied together with an air of effortless avant charm. And she's only refined her approach over the years, delivering a Laurel Canyon-via-Dusseldorf labyrinth of sophisticated juxtapositions on her last album. It was clearly so knotty, in fact, that Holter felt the need to revisit its serene centerpiece 'Materia', rolling out two new versions that triggered this heady, casually brilliant companion album. The rework that started it all, 'Materia 2', isn't some George Lucas affair, either; Holter goes back to the chilly original and genuinely reimagines it, adding a decelerated hypnagogic drum machine pulse that's one part AFX's 'Selected Ambient Works Volume II' and one part Antena's perennial classic 'Camino del Sol'. Holter never loses sight of the initial mystical inspiration, retaining the celestial ecstasy with Laswell-style fretless electric bass and soaring keys as she sings "My heart is loud."

The third version of 'Materia' is more of a bonus track (a self-conscious homage to those mysterious unlisted extras that often appeared on CDs) and finds the divine in languidness, pulling down the tempo and letting the words and harmonies sound out into the empty, reverberant space. But both of these tracks work more like anchors for what's essentially a brand new album; the jerky, 'Hounds of Love'-esque opener 'The Laugh is in the Eyes' is already one of Holter's most inviting, lavish productions. Led by its cannily sculpted rhythm section at first, it flourishes when Holter lets the aesthetic tumult disappear altogether, singing out coolly over weightless pads. And that AFX-cum-Antena influence isn't relegated to the titular redux. The album's lead single 'Fantasy' is an art-pop miracle that sounds as if she's daydreaming over a demo that was passed between Rephlex and Les Disques du Crepuscule before it was lost in the mail some time in the early '90s. It doesn't rest on its laurels either, exploding outwards and somehow integrating tape saturated Walker Brothers-esque psych pop before snapping right back into the groove.

There's a pause for breath on the brief, voice-led 'Clepsydra' before Holter dives headfirst into the extended 'My Twin', the track where she pinched the lead riff she used on 'Fantasy'. When we hear that familiar refrain emerge from near silence, played on an orchestra of broken music boxes and mussed with disorienting pitch and tape delay effects, it's as if we're being scrubbed through someone else's dream. It's one of those tracks that reaffirms why Holter's so good at what she does, composed from a tangled web of ideas and references and sounding somehow effortless at the same time. 'Materia' is Holter at her most whimsical - and most vital.

items._cn_summary: Julia Holter的《Materia》作为2024年专辑的续篇，围绕同名曲目展开重构，衍生出两个新版本。专辑以减速的催眠鼓机脉冲为核心，融合了AFX式环境电子与Antena式梦幻流行质感，无品电贝斯与高亢键盘营造出神圣而眩晕的氛围。作品延续了她对巴洛克流行、高戏剧性与慵懒极简主义的独特调和，开场曲带有《Hounds of Love》式的华丽编排，而单曲《Fantasy》则在艺术流行与磁带饱和的迷幻声响之间自如切换。整体呈现出一种超现实、近乎失重的听觉体验，既保留了对神秘主义灵感的追寻，又在声音细节上不断拓展边界。}

items.body:
The eminently watchable Accidental Meetings introduce extended family member, Lovely Dave, with a real guess-again mixtape (the first in a series) refracting myriad strains of blissed synths, outernational jazz, new wave pop, post punk scuzz, screwed club and dub

Six years into Accidental Meetings’ serendipitous plot, we know to expect anything and everything from the Bristol label, so long as it's got a unique soul and does not bore. Lovely Dave ideally plays true to that brief on his 99 minute mixtape, effortlessly glyding from outernational synth folk to a killer Curtis Mayfield cover via everything from thumb piano meditations, jazz-funked sidewinders, and a proto-new beat bomb on the A-side, before swerving from gothic new wave to smudged minimal wave audities, a pitch-slapped batacuda house ace, and meter-messing skronk on the backside.

Brilliantly strange but true!

items.body:
Enigmatic audity Aisie returns five years on from a strange, overlooked debut with a new suite of compressed atmospheres highly tipped FFO False Aralia, Eliza B.C., Thought Broadcast, Civilistjävel!, Hazyville-era Actress.

‘Black Fire Dream’ picks up from where 2021’s ‘Halcyon Gang Poet’ left us in a surreal, uncanny valley state of mind. The seven part, 30 minute mini-LP continues to fascinate with its cyborganic nature and dreamy otherworldliness, luring down gauzily textured, fractal wormholes where samples of “obscure educational science shows, ghost station radio transmissions, vinyl record detritus and blown-out microscopic field recordings” are gently reanimated and transmuted with a poetic sorcery. 

The whole thing feels as though it were conjuured without human touch, like the inner thoughts of an AI or machines autonomously air-syncing and executing their functions in private. With incremental stealth it breezes by in a hypnagogic haze, half-heard melodies sprouting and dissolving into the aether as granular rhythms buckle and trickle. Eyes will likely be at half mast by the end of the A-side, all the best to receive the B-side’s suggestive, illusive shadowplay of smoke and mirrors refraction and a final slope off into something like a chopped and screwed echo of Topdown Dialectic.

items._cn_summary: 这张七首曲目、约三十分钟的迷你专辑延续了前作超现实与怪诞谷地的氛围，以压缩的声响空间和仿生有机质感构建出梦境般的异世界。素材取自科普节目、幽灵电台广播、黑胶唱片残屑与微观田野录音，经颗粒化节奏与半透明旋律的重新拼合，仿佛由机器自主生成的内心独白。A面在催眠般的薄雾中悄然流逝，半掩的旋律不断萌发又溶解；B面则以烟雾与镜像般的阴影游戏，以及类似 chopped and screwed 的回声效果缓缓收束，整体呈现出一种无人触碰的、私密而疏离的听觉体验。

items.body:
Coltrane’s invigorating ’66 spiritual free jazz salvo - the follow-up to ‘A Love Supreme’ (1965) - is unleashed from the Verve Vault, spotlighting his classic line-up tearing out on templates set by Ornette Coleman years prior, along with more reserved moments of beauty. An evergreen..

"Following the genre-redefining revelations of A Love Supreme in 1965, John Coltrane began a dramatic shift toward spiritual free jazz, abandoning familiar forms in favour of a more abstract sonic palette and bold questions he'd spend the rest of his life and career pursuing. Meditations, released by Impulse! in 1966, continues that emotional throughline while retaining, for the last time in full, the classic quartet that propelled Trane to greatness: pianist McCoy Tyner, bassist Jimmy Garrison and drummer Elvin Jones. (They're further augmented by Pharoah Sanders on tenor sax and additional drummer Rashied Ali.) Meditations pushes Coltrane’s spiritual jazz into heightened realms of energy and abstraction — a powerful document of transformation, intensity, and devotion in Coltrane’s recorded legacy."
items._cn_summary: 这张1966年的专辑是约翰·科川在《A Love Supreme》之后对精神自由爵士的进一步推进，也是他经典四重奏最后一次全员合作的完整记录。音乐在保留 McCoy Tyner、Jimmy Garrison 与 Elvin Jones 所构建的深厚律动与钢琴色彩的同时，引入了 Pharoah Sanders 的次中音萨克斯和 Rashied Ali 的第二套鼓组，使整体声响密度与即兴能量大幅提升。科川在此放弃了熟悉的曲式结构，转向更抽象的音色组合与持续性的集体即兴，在狂烈与静谧之间形成强烈对比。它既是对自由爵士语汇的拓展，也记录了一位艺术家在生命后期对精神性表达的持续追问，是理解其晚期音乐转型的重要文献。

items.body:
Limited edition, first time 2LP re-issue of a compilation originally released via Gary Mundy's legendary Broken Flag imprint in 1987 and featuring a veritable who’s who of post industrial drone and psyche/power electronics including Ramleh, Total, Andrew Chalk and many more.​

"Remastered by Puppy38, this features two bonus tracks not included on the original (and long o/p) LP but only previously found on the even rarer cassette and the equally o/p CD. A timely reminder of this fantastic archive document full of boundary-pushing artists mostly still active in one form or another. Packaged in a sleeve faithful to the distinctive original Cranioclast-designed cover."
items._cn_summary: 这张合辑最初于1987年由Gary Mundy的传奇厂牌Broken Flag发行，此次再版为限量双LP，并经过Puppy38重制，额外收录两首仅存于早期磁带与CD中的附赠曲目。参与者包括Ramleh、Total、Andrew Chalk等，堪称后工业噪音与迷幻电力电子场景的核心阵容。作品以长篇幅的嗡鸣、刺耳反馈和低 fidelity 声响构筑压迫性氛围，体现了八十年代英国地下实验音乐对噪音与黑暗美学的极端探索。专辑保留了Cranioclast设计的原始封面，是对这一重要档案文献的及时回顾，也展示了当时一批突破边界的声音艺术家如何在工业与实验领域持续产生影响。

items.artist: Luke Stewart, Chad Taylor, Aymeric Avice

items.body: In February of 2025, the trio of bassist Luke Stewart, drummer Chad Taylor, and trumpet-playing-electronics-wizard Aymeric Avice gathered in Studio Sextan-La Fonderie in Malakoff, France to make this exciting recording for RogueArt. Having recently performed at Périscope in Lyons, France with drummer Ramon Lopez, Stewart and Avice clearly had chemistry, and would continue to play together with both Lopez and Taylor, including a September 2025 show at the Sons d’hiver festival, a fifteen destination event orbiting Paris that focuses on experimental music, that year operating under the theme of Great Black Music . Check out part of that show here. Deep in the Earth, High in the Sky is a high-energy event. I used the word “exciting” above I think to refer more to how I feel when I listen to the music than to any specific innovation on the part of the trio during this recording. Stewart and Taylor have clearly established themselves as two of THE masters on their respective instruments on the experimental music scene, and here they display sharp and deeply communal listening as they lock-in or open-up with near ESP levels of communication. A good example of this takes place around the three-minute mark of “Pangea Suite #1,” as the two transmute a funk-oriented rock feel into a free improvisation that defies any kind of circular rhythm. Taylor seems to hit his ride cymbal just one time outside of the established backbeat and the two musicians instantaneously take off together into realms unknown. Aymeric Avice, for his part, is just so much fun to listen to, and I fear that I have slept on this musician. Avice is a trumpet virtuoso who lives and plays in electro-sonic amusements. He spends much of his time on this recording swirling and bending the pitches of his trumpet using electronic effects. And, thanks to Avice’s electronic experimentation, often these trumpet pitches come in harmonies wild, fierce, or even a little frightening. “Pangea Suite #2,” for instance features space-age trumpet electronics that can make the listener feel like they are floating in a slightly unreal ether. Check out the three-minute-ish section of this song to hear this levitation. The album is clearly conceived and follows an organized layout. The opening song is “Deep in the Earth,” book-ended by the closing composition “High in the Sky.” Both of these works feature Chad Taylor and Luke Stewart on mbira and are a lovely and meditative introduction and conclusion to the album as a whole. In between these works lie three suites: Pangea Suite , Unknown Suite , and Escaped Sounds , all of which feature the exciting interplay of drums and bass and the electro-experiments of Avice mentioned above. To my ears, the album has two clear reference points. The first is Live-Evil or Bitches Brew era Miles Davis. There are moments in the Unknown Suite , for example, that if cyphoned in ten-second snippets, could have been lifted right from one of these Miles records. “Unknown Suite #2” around 7:30 or 7:40 is evidence of this. The other unmistakable reference point is jaimie branch. jaimie’s mark is all over this album. I mean, goodness, listen to the same song just before and just after the section I referenced above. Avice’s somehow both soft and sinister distortion on the trumpet around six minutes into “Unknown Suite #2” reminds me so much of sections of fly or die. This is to say nothing of the opening of “Unknown Suite #3,” with its ebullient toms, optimistic bass line and trumpet soaring overhead. Even the opening “Deep in the Earth” uses meditative mbira playing reminiscent of some of the beautiful breezy’s work. Of course, part of this connection is because the drummer on this record IS the fly or die drummer. Deep in the Earth, High in the Sky is a fun record to listen to, and is filled with kinetic energy and intuitive interplay. At times serene and moving and at others scorched-earth electronic, this is an album worth checking out. Deep in the Earth, High in the Sky can be found here DEEP IN THE EARTH HIGH IN THE SKY by LUKE STEWART - CHAD TAYLOR - AYMERIC AVICE Email This BlogThis! Share to X Share to Facebook

items._cn_summary: 这张由贝斯手Luke Stewart、鼓手Chad Taylor与兼奏电子的小号手Aymeric Avice组成的三重奏专辑，录制于2025年法国。音乐以高能量即兴为核心，贝斯与鼓展现出近乎心灵感应的默契，能在律动段落与自由即兴之间瞬时转换。小号手大量使用电子效果器，对音高进行扭曲与延展，营造出狂野乃至略带惊悚的和声色彩，部分段落令人联想到漂浮于非现实空间。专辑结构清晰，以两首拇指琴二重奏作为首尾，中间穿插三组组曲，在密集的鼓贝斯互动与电子小号实验中形成张弛有度的叙事。乐评指出其参考点包括Miles Davis的Live-Evil与Bitches Brew时期，尤其在某些即兴片段中能听到明显的传承。整体上这是一次实验爵士与电子声响的深度交汇，展现了三位音乐家在自由即兴框架下的独特协作能力。

From the opening bars of “Chartres” to the closing “La muë,” the album displays an unmistakable coherence of language even when each composition retains its distinct character. items.body: Tapestries brings together works written over more than a decade, yet it never feels like a retrospective. From the opening bars of “Chartres” to the closing “La muë,” the album displays an unmistakable coherence of language even when each composition retains its distinct character. From the architectural “Chartres” to the guttural “Incantare,” from the hallucinatory “Datura” to the metamorphic “La muë,” Justina Repečkaitė‘s music unfolds patiently, asking the listener to focus on the smallest changes in resonance and colour. Its range of references makes this a highly rewarding journey. Medieval stained glass, manuscripts, birdsong, healing charms, poisonous plants and eighteenth-century medical treatises all become starting points for the music. None of these references is treated as programme music or illustration. Instead, Repečkaitė translates them into musical structures that develop according to their own internal logic. The opening “Chartres” immediately establishes this approach. Strings emerge from silence with a cold, almost glacial sonority, creating an acoustic space that expands incrementally. Throughout the album, the ensemble often behaves as a single resonating body rather than a collection of individual instruments. Voices, strings, winds and electronics continually merge, dissolve and reappear, producing a remarkably fluid sound world. One of the album’s most striking works is “Sturnus vulgaris cohibitus.” Inspired by the silence of the pandemic lockdown, Repečkaitė recorded starling calls and plays them back through tiny speakers hidden inside the piano. The electronics become inseparable from the instrument itself, creating the impression that the bird has become trapped within the piano’s resonating body. As the keyboard gradually expands across its register, the birdsong remains dependent on each hammer strike, allowing a simple compositional idea to become a reflection on confinement and the desire to break free. Transformation also lies at the heart of “Datura,” the shortest track on the album. Here the trombonist simultaneously plays, sings and recites botanical descriptions of the poisonous plant whose two principal alkaloids induce either delirium or numbness. Once again, the extended techniques never feel demonstrative. They emerge naturally from the musical idea, allowing the instrument and the voice to occupy the same expressive space. That permeability between voice and instrument runs throughout the album. Singing performers, hybrid timbres and discreet electronics continually broaden the acoustic field. The closing “La muë” brings many of these ideas together. Drawing on an eighteenth-century treatise on the changing adolescent voice, the work combines children’s choir, electronics and the extraordinary sound of the serpent, played and sung simultaneously by Patrick Wibart. Listening to Tapestries, one gradually realises that Repečkaitė is not interested in translating images into music. She is interested in translating systems of thought. Architecture becomes form, birdsong becomes resonance, botanical knowledge becomes gesture, and the changing human voice becomes an evolving sonic landscape. Justina Repečkaitė at Ircam, 2024. Photo Kristijonas Naslenas To expand on the album, Justina Repečkaitė has answered a few questions for us by email. Tapestries spans compositions written between 2012 and 2024 and traces a path from solo works to orchestral and interdisciplinary pieces. Looking back across these twelve years, what threads do you now see connecting these seemingly different works into a single artistic tapestry? I believe that already in “Chartres” (2012) one can recognise the foundations of my musical language, which becomes progressively more complex in “La muë” (2024). My compositions have pre-compositional keys, in the album there is only an exemple of “Chartres”, because its link with the stained glass window is visually speaking. Across the works, different musical parameters are tightly interconnected, often generating a sense of pulsation, cyclical time and organised harmony, governed by arithmetic logic. In purely instrumental pieces such as “Chartres” (2012), “Tapisserie” (2015), and “Vellum” (2020), there are structural affinities in which the ensemble builds a shared architectural form, rather than a collection of individual parts, individualities. This architectural thinking also persists in “La Cité des Dames” (2018) and in the vocal writing of “La Muë”, though there it is articulated through the presence of text – whether as resistance in “La Cité des Dames” or transformation in “La Muë”. Another recurring thread is the permeability between voice and instrument. My instrumental writing is often described as vocal, while my vocal writing is conceived in a similarly instrumental manner. Singing while playing the instruments appears in several works: the trombone in “Datura” (2021), the serpent in “La Muë” (2024), and the flute in “Incantare” (2018). Even “Sturnus vulgaris cohibitus” can be understood as “singing,” since its electronics are derived from a short starling song that resonates with and colours every piano gesture. In the works with electronics, its function is an expansion of the instrument, opening its acoustic space and extending its resonance. More broadly, many of my works reference manuscripts, traditions, or historical practices because they feed my imagination. Architectural and visual forms appear throughout your work, from the stained glass of “Chartres” to the textile references of “Tapisserie” and the manuscript imagery of “Vellum”. What attracts you to these material and architectural metaphors, and how do they influence your compositional thinking? Before I turned to composition, I was preparing to study visual arts, so my artistic education was rooted in images rather than in music. That background has never disappeared. I have a particular fascination with the medieval world, where architecture, manuscripts and textiles reveal systems in which proportion, number and geometry generate beauty. As a composer who often works with rigorous underlying structures, I find it inspiring to see how rules and constraints can produce forms of remarkable richness and expressivity. These references are therefore more than poetic metaphors or title inspirations. They influence how I conceive musical form. I am inspired by the idea that a score might possess an autonomous existence, almost like an architectural drawing, a textile pattern or a draft manuscript: a carefully constructed object whose internal organisation embodies ideas before it is ever brought into sound. I carefully craft the pre-compositional keys of my works, as they gather the essential logic and structure of a piece on a single page, like a blueprint of the musical form. Voice occupies a special place in your music. In “Incantare,” “Datura,” and “La muë,” performers sing while playing their instruments, creating hybrid timbres that blur the boundary between body and instrument. What first drew you to this technique, and what does it allow you to express that conventional instrumental writing cannot? I first experimented with simultaneous singing and playing technique while writing Toro (2015) for electronics and the euphonium player Vianney Desplantes, who taught me a great deal about it. What interests me in this fusion of sounds is the emergence of a hybrid timbre, in which the boundary between body and instrument becomes porous. The voice is the most intimate instrument, and when it is projected through another instrument, it produces a very personal and unstable sound – never identical from one performer to another! As I am also a singer, I do not separate vocal production from instrumental sound; for me they belong to the same continuum of expression. For example, Incantare has been performed by both male and female flutists, across different vocal ranges and instruments, and each interpretation reveals a distinct version of the piece. In this sense, the work exists less as a fixed object than as a living transformation shaped by performers. Several pieces transform non-musical materials into musical structures: Lithuanian healing charms in Incantare, birdsong in “Sturnus vulgaris cohibitus,” Christine de Pizan’s feminist text in “La Cité des Dames,” and an eighteenth-century treatise on puberty in “La muë.” How do you approach the process of translating historical, literary, or natural phenomena into sound? The pieces you mention were written during moments of intense creative momentum. I found the ideas behind them so compelling that the process often felt less like inventing something from nothing and more like uncovering something that was already present. The initial spark of Incantare (2018), La Cité des Dames (2019) , Sturnus vulgaris cohibitus (2020), and La muë (2024) was so strong that my role as a composer was to reveal and shape its musical potential. For me, music is not separate from other cultural or natural forms; rather, it is a space where they can be transformed and reconfigured into sound. I am not interested in illustrating a text, a historical source, or a natural phenomenon, but in identifying the structures, gestures, rhythms, materials, and energies within them that can generate a musical language of their own. This is perhaps why I never use a text in its entirety, but rather extract fragments that contain the essential qualities I want to transform through composition. “La Cité des Dames” draws on Christine de Pizan’s visionary text about creating a symbolic city for women, while “La muë” explores transformation through adolescence, voice, and bodily change. Do questions of identity, gender, and embodiment play a broader role in your work, even when they are not explicitly foregrounded? In these two pieces, identity is primordial. In “La Cité des Dames,” Christine de Pizan’s text describes women creating a symbolic space of their own in a society where their voices were marginalized. The fact that the work is written for six soprano parts makes the female voice itself part of its meaning. In La muë, the subject is the adolescent voice changing during puberty. The voice becomes a marker of bodily transformation and identity. The child singers, the serpent player who sings through the instrument, and the electronics all expand the relationship between body, instrument, and sound. Beyond these two works, I am often interested in states of transition, where change is still unfolding. This is true both conceptually and at the smallest level of my music, where repetition is never static but constantly transformed through timbre, dynamics, and context. In “La Cité des Dames” and “La muë,” the body and voice become central because they are themselves sites of transformation: the collective female voice reclaiming a space of expression in the former, and the changing adolescent voice in the latter. Your music is often described as balancing rigorous construction with organic, almost living sonic processes. One critic compared your compositions to cycles of germination, growth, blossoming, and decay. Do you think of your works primarily as structures to be built, or as organisms that evolve according to their own internal logic? I begin with rigorously constructed structures, and then let the musical material grow organically within them. The structuring process can be demanding, sometimes involving the abandonment of many ideas, but once the framework is in place, the music begins to move freely inside it, as if the architecture itself begins to sing. (Gianmarco Del Re)

items._cn_summary: 这张专辑汇集了作曲家十余年间的作品，却呈现出高度统一的声音语言。音乐灵感来自中世纪彩窗、手稿、鸟鸣、治疗咒语、有毒植物与十八世纪医学论文，但并未沦为标题性描绘，而是被转化为遵循内在逻辑的音响结构。弦乐、人声、管乐与电子不断融合、消散、重组，形成流动的共鸣场域。《Sturnus vulgaris cohibitus》将椋鸟叫声通过微型扬声器置于钢琴内部，使鸟鸣与琴槌击弦互为依存，隐喻封锁中的困顿与挣脱；《Datura》中长号手同时演奏、演唱并朗诵植物学描述，扩展技法自然嵌入音乐肌理；终曲《La muë》结合童声合唱、电子与同时演奏和演唱的蛇形管，呼应变声期论著。整张专辑以细腻的声响变化和跨媒介的创作视角，构建出兼具建筑感与幻觉感的聆听体验。

items.body: If you’re a regular reader here, you’d know by now what I search for the most in new music is something that I’ve never heard before. BJ Cole and Secondson’s new pedal steel guitar and Cristal Baschet duo record, There is Wonder Here, is exactly that. Available 9/18 from Centripetal Force on CD, vinyl and digital (and on cassette through Geology Records), this album is a dreamy and otherworldly set of soundscapes and experimental compositions that break through the boundaries of ambient Americana music into something completely new and original. So what makes this album so particularly unique? Well, for starters, BJ Cole is one of the most groundbreaking and influential pedal steel players ever, known for mastering and expanding the horizons of his instrument through collaborations with the likes of The Orb, Björk, John Cale and Brian Eno (plus famously appearing on Elton John’s “Tiny Dancer,”). Yet it’s his distinctive approach to the instrument combined with the utterly incomparable sound of the Cristal Baschet that makes this LP stand apart from anything else you might find in the record shop today. Seen here in this image that I absolutely borrowed from Wikipeida A Cristal Baschet is sort of like a glass harmonica, with gentle, vocal-like tones and great oscillating Cathedral pipe organ-like resonances that are produced by rubbing chromatically tuned glass rods with wet fingertips. Secondson has described the rare instrument as “an acoustic synthesizer,” and its ghostly drones and shimmering tones blend sympathetically with the similarly sweeping, ethereal sounds of the pedal steel. When played together, the effect is expansive, transfixing and downright moving. Photo by Rhodri Brooks Photo by Rhodri Brooks While you might expect music from this particular combination of instruments to be purely minimal and amorphous, you’d be surprised to find that these tracks are actual songs with melodies and tight structures. Check out “A Place You Could Never Leave,” the album’s first single, for example: With the way this track sways, dances and ebbs and flows, it’s almost lyrical. This particular song, and several others on this record, even has the vibe of a grand orchestral piecee that echoes the work of some of the more progressive modernist American classical composers of the 20th century. Fans of North Americans, Keith Jarrett’s Hymns/Spheres and Mark Korven’s soundtrack to Robert Eggers’ The Lighthouse will surely appreciate the beauty and genius of this duo record. Click here to preorder your copy today. -KH
items._cn_summary: 这张专辑由踏板钢棒吉他手BJ Cole与Cristal Baschet演奏者Secondson合作，以两种罕见乐器构成二重奏。Cristal Baschet被描述为“声学合成器”，通过湿手指摩擦调音玻璃棒产生类似人声与管风琴的共振，与踏板钢棒的滑音和延音交织，形成迷幻、空旷的声音景观。尽管乐器组合实验性强，但作品并非纯氛围碎片，而是具有旋律和紧凑结构的歌曲，例如单曲《A Place You Could Never Leave》带有管弦乐般的起伏与律动。评论者认为它突破了ambient Americana的边界，并联想到北美民谣、Keith Jarrett的《Hymns/Spheres》以及Mark Korven为《灯塔》所做的配乐。专辑由Centripetal Force发行，提供CD、黑胶、数字和磁带版本。

items.body: Gelareh Pour and Brian O’Dwyer build each show live, on the spot, from a kamancheh, a voice, and a drum kit. Nine years into the project, that’s made them genuinely hard to predict, even for themselves. Pour grew up in Iran, where the path to a singing career ran through very narrow lanes for a woman; she carried that instrument and that history with her to Australia, where she met O’Dwyer, a drummer with a strong ear for improvisation and a real curiosity about where Persian tradition could go next. Together they’ve picked up an Art Music Award for Excellence in Experimental Practice in 2024, and travelled to the Banff Centre for Arts and Creativity in Canada to record their third album in a single live pass, each take committed to tape as it happened. Its title, May The Devil’s Ear Be Deaf, comes from an old Persian phrase spoken after voicing something beautiful, a quiet ritual to protect fragile, precious things from envy. Vulnerability like that runs through everything ZÖJ do. Nothing is rehearsed, nothing is fixed after the fact, and once a performance is out in the room it belongs to whoever is listening. That’s how we want to start this year’s Musical Road to WOMEX: with two musicians who make something delicate in front of an audience and then hand it over, so that what happens in Las Palmas will exist only for the people in that room.  ZÖJ means “pair”, and your music is a conversation — kamancheh, voice and drums, largely improvised. For a first-time listener, how would you describe what happens between you on stage? Every ZÖJ performance begins with listening. Before there is sound, there is attention, to each other, to the room, to the audience, to the things that cannot be planned. We don’t approach the stage with a fixed script; we bring our shared musical language and trust. Then we allow the music to reveal itself in the moment. We don’t think of the kamancheh, voice and drums as accompanying one another, more so they’re in conversation. Sometimes they whisper, sometimes they challenge, sometimes they leave space for silence to speak. Our approach to and use of improvisation allows us to be completely present, and that presence becomes something we share with everyone in the room. The audience isn’t only watching the performance; they’re part of shaping its energy. No two concerts are ever the same because no gathering of people is ever the same. Gelareh, you grew up as a girl in Iran where a professional life in music wasn’t an option, and you’ve since made it your whole world across two countries. What in that journey most shapes ZÖJ’s sound? Growing up in Iran, I was surrounded by music. I attended concerts, listened deeply, and was inspired by extraordinary musicians. But as a girl, I also understood from an early age that there were limits on what a musical future could look like for me. Singing publicly as a woman wasn’t a path that was open to me, and that awareness shaped the way I related to music as something precious that had to be protected and pursued with determination. Migrating to Australia gave me the freedom to explore music without those constraints, while carrying with me everything I had learned in Iran. Rather than leaving one world behind for another, ZÖJ lives in the conversation between them. My Iranian heritage, my research into women’s voices in diaspora, and Brian’s openness as an improviser come together in a space where memory meets discovery. I think that’s what most defines our sound: it’s not about choosing between cultures or traditions, but allowing them to meet with honesty, curiosity and deep listening. The Canary Islands are their own crossing of worlds: a Berber Indigenous root, Spanish layers on top, and deep ties to Latin America through centuries of migration. As a duo whose music is about belonging to more than one place, what can that kind of mixed identity mean at this particular moment in history? Mixed identities aren’t exceptions; they’re one of the defining experiences of our time. Most of us carry multiple histories, languages and homes within us. Those intersections aren’t something fragmented, they’re places of creativity and possibility. Music has always travelled more freely than borders allow, and it reminds us that cultures have always been shaped through exchange. The Canary Islands feel like a place where many currents meet. That makes it an especially meaningful setting for WOMEX, because the festival itself celebrates dialogue rather than division. At a time when the world often asks us to choose one identity over another, we’re interested in making music that embraces complexity and connection. Your music is improvisation-based: no two ZÖJ concerts alike, with the audience as a third point of the triangle. In a WOMEX programme full of traditions, what makes that approach distinctly yours, and what do you hope people take from it? We’re deeply rooted in tradition, but we don’t treat tradition as something fixed. The Persian musical language I draw from has always had improvisation at its heart, and we bring that into conversation with contemporary expression, original compositions, and the unique dynamic conversation we’ve developed as a duo. What makes ZÖJ distinctive is that improvisation isn’t a section of the performance, it is the performance. We don’t begin with the intention of reproducing a recording or presenting a definitive version of a piece. We trust the relationship between us, the atmosphere of the room, and the presence of the audience to shape where the music goes. We are creating in real-time, not reciting a learned repertoire. We hope people leave feeling that music can be a living conversation rather than a finished product. If our performance encourages someone to listen more openly, to sound, to silence, to each other, or to their own inner world, then we’ve achieved something meaningful. WOMEX always sparks unexpected meetings. Are there particular artists or showcases you’re looking forward to in Las Palmas? One of the things we love most about festivals is discovering artists we didn’t know we needed to hear. Some of the most memorable musical encounters happen completely by chance. We’re especially looking forward to seeing Nana Benz Du Togo again. We first saw them at WOMADelaide in Australia, and we were so captivated that, while we were standing there watching their set, we bought their record online before the concert had even finished. More broadly, we’re excited by artists who are deeply grounded in their own traditions while remaining open to dialogue and exchange. WOMEX has a remarkable way of bringing those people together, and we’re looking forward as much to the conversations between showcases as the performances themselves. 6Your work asks for deep, patient listening and treats the audience as a collaborator. How does a room of delegates — and an unfamiliar space — shape a ZÖJ set? An unfamiliar space sharpens our listening. We don’t try to make every venue feel the same. We’d rather allow the room to become part of the instrument. The acoustics, the atmosphere, the attention of the audience, all of these influence the music. A room full of delegates can be wonderfully energising because everyone arrives carrying different musical histories. Our hope is that, for a little while, those different backgrounds dissolve into a shared experience of listening. That’s where real connection begins. You’ve spoken about nature feeding directly into your music, the moon, the horizon, the wind in the leaves. What’s your relationship to place and landscape in what you write, and is there anything about a volcanic Atlantic island like Gran Canaria you’re hoping to take in while you’re there? Nature reminds us how to listen. The rhythms of wind, tides, birds, light and silence have always been big influences. We don’t try to imitate nature, but we do try to remember that we’re part of it. We’re looking forward to walking Gran Canaria’s coastline, watching the Atlantic horizon, and spending time with the landscape. Gelareh, your research and your art both centre Iranian women’s voices in diaspora. Is there a message you feel especially compelled to carry through this showcase, at this moment? My work has always been about making space for voices that have too often been unheard. Iranian women have shown extraordinary courage, resilience and creativity, both inside Iran and across the diaspora. Rather than speaking for them, I hope our music creates space where their strength, complexity and humanity can be felt. At a time when many people are displaced by conflict, oppression or circumstance, I hope this showcase reminds us that every migration carries stories, knowledge and beauty, not only pain. Listening deeply to those stories is an act of solidarity. Beyond WOMEX, now that May The Devil’s Ear Be Deaf is out, what’s next for the duo? New writing, touring, collaborations, a direction you haven’t tried yet? We’re excited to let May The Devil’s Ear Be Deaf continue finding its audience through touring and live performance, because that’s where the music keeps evolving. Alongside that, we are always recording new material that continues to explore improvisation, storytelling and the meeting of musical traditions. We’re always open to collaborations with artists from different cultural and artistic backgrounds, particularly where there’s genuine curiosity in communication. If you could write a personal invitation to the people of Las Palmas to come and discover your showcase, what would it say? Dear friends, We would love to meet you through music. If you come to our concert, you won’t hear a performance that has been repeated many times before. You’ll hear something that exists only in that room, on that evening, created together with everyone present. Bring your curiosity. Bring your imagination. Bring your silence as well as your applause. Let’s discover what becomes possible when we truly listen to one another. See you in Las Palmas.   ZÖJ play WOMEX 2026's Official Showcase Selection in Las Palmas de Gran Canaria, 21–25 October     PLAYLIST: ZÖJ X RHYTHM PASSPORT   You can find all the previous episodes of Musical Road to Womex HERE   The post Musical Road to WOMEX 2026 – ZÖJ appeared first on Rhythm Passport.

items._cn_summary: ZÖJ是伊朗音乐家Gelareh Pour与澳大利亚鼓手Brian O'Dwyer的即兴二重奏，以卡曼切琴、人声和鼓组在舞台上实时构建音乐。他们摒弃预设脚本，通过聆听与对话让作品在当下生成，强调现场氛围与观众共同塑造的不可复制的瞬间。第三张专辑在加拿大班夫中心以一次性现场录制完成，标题源自波斯语中用以保护美好事物免受嫉妒的古老短语，透露出作品中的脆弱与珍重。Pour的伊朗成长背景与女性歌唱经验为音乐注入独特的文化厚度，而O'Dwyer的即兴直觉则让波斯传统乐声与当代鼓组产生开放性的碰撞。该组合曾获2024年澳大利亚艺术音乐奖实验实践卓越奖，其创作路径兼具文化根源与实验精神，适合关注即兴、世界融合与跨文化声音探索的听众。

items.body: I’ve seen the most magical of all magical rhythm sections in free jazz / improvised music - John Edwards on double bass and Mark Sanders on drums - several times now, the first time as the Foils Quartet with Frank Paul Schubert on saxophone and Matthias Müller on trombone. I was immediately blown away; my jaw literally kept dropping at the musical fireworks the two of them set off. Later, I saw them with Trevor Watts and Veryan Weston, then with Swiss saxophonist Omri Ziegele, and finally, three years ago, with John Butcher. However, the most spectacular gig was a concert with Roscoe Mitchell at the Météo Festival in Mulhouse in 2016. After ten minutes, the audience jumped to their feet and gave a standing ovation, yelling, shouting in pure ecstasy - right in the middle of the piece. Sometimes I think that even a way below-average amateur guitarist like me could play with them, and the result would be - let’s say - not a complete disaster. Because It Happens is part of a gig at Café Oto (the other part, Not So Late , is available on a separate CD), and for this recording, the rhythm twins have enlisted the help of first class Polish saxophonist and bass clarinetist Mikołaj Trzaska. It’s no surprise that the trio is in full swing from the very first seconds,. Sanders stays firmly on the drums, which lends the improvisation a dark, driving character. Trzaska uses this for insanely fast runs, which are nonetheless underpinned by a deep spirituality. Many influences converge in his playing: Coltrane, Brötzmann, Shepp, Parker, and many more. His style is both energetic and subtle, he uses vibrato when appropriate but he can also sound very dry and abstract. Added to this is his excellent timing that leaves plenty of space for Edwards and Sanders. All of this is evident right from the opener “Running Loose”. Throughout the entire set a wide range of emotions is explored; there are moments of intense density followed by very lyrical passages (e.g., in “Creator of Creatures”) and superbly integrated solos (see Sanders’s drum solo in “Written By”). However, the highlight of the album is the encore, “Light Inches”, which Edwards and Sanders kick off with an off-the-wall rhythm. The piece swings back and forth, Trzaska lets the notes dart through the room, breaks off abruptly, plays somewhere in the background, then Edwards takes the lead - the three musicians seem to be arguing over the direction of the improvisation, only to then agree almost instinctively on where to go. The rest is sheer madness in terms of power, harmony, and perfection. Because It Happens is an outstanding album in every respect. Anyone who wants to hear state-of-the-art European free jazz (or “live composition”, as the musicians call it) should give this release a try. Because It Happens is available on vinyl and as a download. Because It Happens by Mikołaj Trzaska, John Edwards, Mark Sanders Email This BlogThis! Share to X Share to Facebook
items._cn_summary: 这张专辑录制于伦敦Café Oto的现场演出，由波兰萨克斯与低音单簧管演奏家Mikołaj Trzaska携手英国即兴节奏双人组John Edwards与Mark Sanders共同完成。音乐从开场便进入高度紧张的即兴状态，鼓手Sanders保持稳固而暗黑的驱动性节奏，为Trzaska急速的旋律线条提供坚实基底。Trzaska的演奏融合了Coltrane、Brötzmann、Shepp等前辈的影响，既有爆发力十足的快速跑动，也具备干燥抽象的音响控制，同时以精准的留白为贝斯与鼓创造对话空间。整场演出在密集的声响与抒情的段落之间来回摆动，如《Creator of Creatures》中展现出难得的静谧气质，而加演曲《Light Inches》则呈现三人围绕即兴方向展开的激烈拉扯与默契合流。乐评认为这是一张代表当代欧洲自由爵士前沿水准的录音，体现了乐手所称的“活作曲”理念，在能量、和声与完满度上均达到极高层次。

items._cn_summary: Cornelius时隔三年推出新作《Refractions》，以“屈折”为题，在看似对立的元素间构建微妙平衡。乐评指出，专辑同时容纳无意义与意味深长、保守与攻击、电子节拍与放克律动、人性化与冷彻感，并通过明显的立体声像、精细设定的残响与细碎编辑制造出多层次的凹凸质感。这种极端的共存并未导向晦涩，反而呈现出高度流行化的听感，体现出创作者深厚而广阔的音乐背景。此外，专辑收录了井上阳水《梦寝见》的翻唱，延续了前作《梦中梦》的脉络。整体而言，这是一张在实验性与可听性之间取得罕见平衡的作品，适合关注声音细节与结构张力的听众深入探索。
