items.body: Deep utterances and smoky melodies fill the old courtyards of Jozef Van Wissem’s music. On Nobody Living Can Ever Make Me Turn Back (Consouling Sounds), the lute’s spidery melodies appear as finely woven webs, echoing into the present from the distant past. Something is brewing. An explosive beat rocks the medieval sound to its core, less a queasy shake and more like a 7.o earthquake. The misty and quietly revolutionary tones carry the ill weight of death. The melodies themselves are almost like the Black Death, spreading throughout the eastern European townships of the album and going door-to-door, knocking lightly like a strange, dark-coated preacher – ‘you will come with me now’, it says – as the sickening fog leaves behind nothing but stark, quiet streets and stained doors, a field of hastily-painted crosses traced along both sides. Clammy-faced inhabitants are locked inside otherwise empty rooms, and a row of filled tombs line the music, track by track. There is something incredibly earthy to the sound, like century-old soil. Nobody Living Can Ever Make Me Turn Back takes its inspiration from a painting by Belgian artist Cindy Wright (her painting is the one on the cover). Things are delicate here, as delicate and as temporary as a note on a quivering string before it fades into permanent silence, into its flame-streaked sunset, ultimately moving into the death of itself and its subsequent absorption into the earth and air. Nothing lasts forever, and the skull on the cover testifies to that. Van Wissem’s music plucks a very distinct chord. The notes are splayed out like an ancient victim on a medieval rack, but there’s more of an emphasis on pleasure rather than on pain, with echoing vocals calling out from a cold, lantern-lit chamber, soaking into the cold slabs of stone, and the masterful playing of the lute ringing through the draughty corridors. At other times, the lute appears stately and dignified, resplendent in a magnificent, proud set of robes. But the sparse arrangement, as well as the concentrated focus on one instrument, ensures that beneath the robed appearance there lies a body that’s thin bordering on the anorexic or even the skeletal, despite a flurry of faster passages that seem to run at quite a pace and with a good deal of urgency. The notes are still as narrow as a spindle, and that’s just a characteristic of the lute. Pockets of light are able to shine weakly out from the brighter tracks, offering a pale, stained-glass-window light. There are other reinterpretations of death here, too: a death of a nation as the British PM makes a suicidal statement. But the rose is still beautiful even as it dies. The future has and always will be an uncertain unknown, but willingly jumping off the edge without first looking down or checking to see where you’re going seems to be neither a sane nor reasonable course of action. Nobody Living Can Ever Make Me Turn Back revels in its uncertainty and in its transient nature. It began as dust, and to dust it returns. www.consouling.be
items._cn_summary: Jozef Van Wissem以鲁特琴为核心，构建出一片弥漫着死亡气息的中世纪声响景观。专辑灵感源自比利时画家Cindy Wright的画作，音符如蛛网般细密交织，在古老庭院与阴冷石廊间回响。乐评强调其音乐兼具精致与腐朽感，稀疏编曲中透出近乎骷髅般的瘦削质地，而偶尔爆发的节拍则如地震般撼动古旧的氛围。暗色调中亦有微弱光线透出，整体游走于愉悦与痛苦、优雅与衰败之间，并以不确定性和短暂性为乐。作品将古代乐器置于当代实验语境中，融合暗潮与古典余韵，形成极具辨识度的个人声响，值得深入聆听。

items.body: The World Unseen The delayed glow of a late summer’s light and its piercing, beatific atmosphere surrounds the music of Mamiffer (Faith Coloccia and Aaron Turner). Sublime incantations, powerful, sweeping movements and slow hymns cycle in and around a contained vacuum of sound, its choral music left in a dusty, unclean state with its soot-tinted touch of decaying beauty. The sung passages are a slice of heaven, but the music is more like Paradise Lost. Rougher static prickles against the skin, and the lines that separate the living from the dead get thinner and thinner as The World Unseen progresses; a supernatural occurrence waits on the other side, one that only those who have passed over can see. The atmosphere enveloping the music is despondent, crestfallen and perhaps inevitable as it stands dressed in black at the tombstone of one so beloved. The music decays and darkens in real time as life fades away and the river that leads into death is crossed. The lifeblood oozes out of the body and into crimson pools over which blackened boats, crafted with sharp blades and skeletal thin in their appearance and in their construction, constantly rock from side to side as they slowly travel beyond the veil, from one dimension to the next. Things take somewhat of a left turn, and when the sun sets it gets dark really quickly. As pinpoint as the thin, sighted accuracy of a laser beam, the light cuts through anything that attempts to block it. The electric guitars are caged in a low tuning, growling close to the ground, juddering and shuddering against the doors of doom and heavy sludge but never quite breaking them down and succumbing to their lower descent. The piano of ‘Mara’ ghosts around them, the emptiness surrounding the music completely. A bruising, harder edge sits on the music’s shoulders, riding with it around a once-pristine prairie on the edge of the badlands. In three parts, ‘Domestication of the Ewe’ forgoes the radiating harmonies and is instead a complete and utter blackout. Its heavy weight becomes an oppressive burden as black as midnight television, its static crawling and seeming to speak from beyond the confines of these old, decrepit walls. The crawling lines and dots are an ancient power, and they become ever more potent during the midnight hour. As Coloccia says, “the record is imperfect…it has within its heart an incompleteness, a stillness containing the presence of absence and loss.” And through the whispered, gentle singing, that loss hangs there as something eternal, written on the sheet music of a life right until the coda, perpetually dancing between the two extremes of order and chaos, the two uniting forces in dominating control of the universe, where a sudden, seemingly unpredictable shock of a violating act of violence is mingled with the everlasting beauty of this rock we call Earth. It is a bruised beauty. It is The World Unseen. “If you must have a language, let it be one whose quantity cannot be reduced to a single sound, one that moves without displacing, that describes without being written, that knows the letter and yet is the spirit and has the spirit to be without recourse to visibility, that is made of time and not altered by time, that knows neither childhood or age, neither the tongues or the teeth that gnaw at foreign languages, that gives birth to itself, whose soul is everywhere and nowhere, that is free in its coupling. Air cut out of air… a motive force of infinity… and the world will be music… where birth and death overlap.” – Hélén Cixous www.sigerecords.blogspot.co.uk
items._genre: experimental / dark ambient / drone / post-metal / avant-garde
items._cn_summary: 这张专辑以迟缓的夏日余晖般的氛围开场，将圣咏式人声置于灰烬与静电之中，营造出衰败而神圣的声响空间。钢琴与低音吉他在沉重与虚无间游移，时而浮现厄运金属般的压迫感，却始终未彻底坠入泥泞。三乐章作品《Domestication of the Ewe》则完全放弃和谐共鸣，转为近乎彻底的黑暗，以爬行的噪音与古老符号般的点线暗示超验力量。整体听感如同在生与死的边界摆渡，从微光到全黑，从秩序到混沌，最终凝结为一种淤青般的残缺之美。其独特之处在于将宗教音乐般的庄严感与实验噪音的粗糙质地结合，使缺失与死亡成为可触摸的实体，值得深入聆听。

items.body: Palagoma is not only the first release from Nairobi-based label Cool Waters, it also marks the first time German-born, Kenya-based percussionist Sven Kacirek has collaborated with Ogoya Nengo and Olith Ratengo at the same time. Odd Okoddo, the duo of Kacirek and Ratengo, has been performing since 2018, but with the inclusion of the 83 year old Nengo, a singer from the eastern part of the country, there�s an added traditional depth to the music. A 2025 performance shows Nengo�s lifetime of experience singing Kenya�s dodo tradition around 2 and half minutes in (see below). Furthermore, her inclusion on this album allows her and Ratengo to toss the vocals back and forth as they reference their shared roots (Ratengo and Nengo live minutes from each other). Musically, however, the tracks are driven by Kacirek�s Buchla synth, hand percussion, and occasional kit drumming, which serve to buoy the voices without blotting out the music�s origins. Palagoma by Odd Okoddo & Ogoya Nengo �Bara,� for example, begins with the dime-store thwack of a repeated pattern, a stiff juxtaposition to the voices; yet, as the song rolls along, a 4/4 clink appears, then a burbling bass, and finally, what sounds like a xylophone. Layers of synthesized polyrhythms keep presenting themselves with a subtlety almost unnoticeable, until, by the track�s end, it feels organic, as if it�s all been underneath the two voices all along. Palagoma by Odd Okoddo & Ogoya Nengo �Sarah,� perhaps the album�s most intense track, features a lead vocal from Ratengo and tentative, percussive spittles from Kacirek. And while the technology never tries to overtake the vocals, it does sneak up and punctuate the track�s urgency, as edgy distortion sneaks in here and there just as Ratengo�s voice reaches its peak. The term �folktronica� has been bandied about as a way to house the type of music on offer here. In fact, exploratory collaborations such as Chouk Bwa & The �ngstr�mers as well as much of Kampala, Uganda�s Nyege Nyege label house sounds that might be �folktronic� in some way. What�s more interesting and important about this music, though, is how truly global so much of it is while maintaining a deep connection to Africa and its diasporic communities. The music on Palagoma , as well as much of what�s linked above (and available in countless other recent recordings) demonstrates a real willingness for cultures to respond to each other without trampling traditions altogether. Instead, roots become avant-garde and innovations become seemingly thousands of years old. Certainly the inclusion of an 83 year old traditional Kenyan singer only recently making her global debut as she tours with a duo whose instrumental voice is a white male saturated in electronic Kenyan rhythms demonstrates this blurring. The music this trio makes is certainly of the 21st century, but it�s often hazy, sparse, and open, keeping it from a quick sell-by date or confining it to a specific genre. Instead, it�s a beautiful example music as grace.
items.label: Cool Waters
items._genre: folktronica / experimental electronic / world fusion / avant-garde
items._cn_summary: 这张专辑由德国出生、肯尼亚定居的打击乐手Sven Kacirek与肯尼亚歌手Ogoya Nengo、Olith Ratengo组成的三重奏录制，是内罗毕厂牌Cool Waters的首张出品。Nengo以83岁高龄带来肯尼亚dodo传统演唱，与Ratengo的嗓音相互呼应；Kacirek用Buchla合成器、手打击乐和套鼓构建层层叠叠的复节奏，在电子声响与传统人声之间形成微妙渗透。开篇曲《Bara》从生硬重复的节奏逐渐长出4/4拍金属声、低音与类似木琴的音色，使合成器织体听起来仿佛一直潜藏于人声之下；《Sarah》则以失真音色和打击乐碎片强化紧迫感。作品既保留非洲根源，又让传统在21世纪电子语境中转化为前卫声音。

I want to personally direct you to a remarkable piece of music titled "Two Views of a Prayer," composed and written by
David Dzubinski
as part of the
Prism Quartet
's new series of collaborations called
Unlocking Your Inner Composer
. If you have listened to my radio programs, you are probably familiar with the quartet's ground-breaking, genre-blurring music. If not, there's no better introduction than this.
Performed in November of 2025 at the Free Library of Philadelphia, they invited vocalist
Ursula Rucker
, percussionist
Tyshawn Sorey
, and violinist
Carlos Santiago
to collaborate on the arrangement and performance of Dzubinski's composition. It travels from raw to lyrical and back in the course of just under 4 minutes, with both finesse and energy. - Cliff Furnald, editor

items._cn_summary: 棱镜四重奏的“解锁你内心的作曲家”合作系列推出大卫·祖宾斯基创作的《祈祷的两种视角》。作品于2025年11月在费城自由图书馆演出，邀请人声厄苏拉·鲁克、打击乐泰肖恩·索雷与小提琴卡洛斯·圣地亚哥共同参与编曲和演奏。全曲不到四分钟，在粗粝与抒情之间来回转换，兼具控制力与即兴能量。棱镜四重奏以打破类型边界著称，这次合作把萨克斯四重奏的合奏传统与即兴、人声、打击乐和小提琴的对话结合起来，在短小篇幅内形成密集的声响变化。其价值在于将多位不同背景的即兴者纳入作曲框架，让作品既有结构又保持现场协作的张力。

items.body: Sendas by Omar Sosa True to a Monk-inspired commitment never to play the same thing twice, Cuban pianist and composer Omar Sosa�s Sendas (Pathways), his latest solo offering, is the vivid invention of a pensive, restlessly creative, evolutionary artistry. As with all Sosa�s work, Sendas is the fortunate product of serendipity. In 2021 the COVID lockdown was underway, his marriage was ending, and a scheduled Milan appearance cancellation garnered an invitation to record at the Fazioli Pianoforti Concert Hall, annex to the renowned Italian piano manufactory in Sacile, Pordenone, about an hour northeast of Venice. At Fazioli, Sosa found himself in august company. Herbie Hancock and a host of classical pianists are Fazioli artists. Among the institutions that have embraced the Fazioli sound are the Juilliard School, Teatro La Fenice (Venice), the Budapest Palace of Arts, the Paris Conservatory, the Beijing Grand Theatre, and the universities of Salzburg, Graz, and Vienna. An unscripted two-hour solo improvisation on a Fazioli grand in the empty concert hall provided the raw audio for Sendas , later to be flavored in the mix, sparsely, with voice clips, percussion, loops, field recordings, found sounds effects that Sosa has collected over a career spanning four decades. As Sosa related to me soon after completing the post-production of Sendas , �Humanity is spiritually lost. We humans are all in this together. We need to evolve, but always keeping the traditions, walking with a strong, determined pace. We need more grounded music with overtones that resonate with the lower chakras� like throat singing, a mantra of the universal music.� �Creativity is about combining all your influences in a new way. I don�t aspire to be jazz, Latin, timba, reggaeton, classical. I avoid styles, but I respect the forms.� �I try not to think about how listeners will receive it but I do try to address their expectations, and go with the music to some other new place. Many free spirits come to listen, to be a part of the journey we are on.� Sosa laughs, �My son says, �Your niche is really small.� But the people who come really are there to be part of what we are going to do.� �Economics, technology, the streaming ear wash, algorithms all want to put you into a defined category � and so do many music journalists! The industry�s mentality is that any investment in artists must be defined by market categories to be profitable.� �But I play to be free of that,� Sosa says. �I play without thinking. There are no wrong notes. I love the first take. That�s the take, the natural voice of your soul. �Less is more� is a mantra in my life and music.� Consider the opening of �Inside the Spirit,� easing in leisurely, reaching over the keyboard into the resonant heart of the instrument, plucking and stroking the strings, teasing out a fuller resonance � only later to be embellished in the studio mix with light percussion and the muted Spanish-language refrain of a pregonero or street vendor, as might be heard in the calles of Havana or any other Latin American barrio. Sendas by Omar Sosa Moving from the secular to the sacred, �Deities Serenade� is an Afro-Cuban invocation of the shape-shifting divine, yet with ample room for ecumenical recasting in accord with a listener�s own self-location. �Inside My Soul� and �Something from Home� are Sosa works that to my ear may be an intuitive response to the distant call of Chopin�s "Nocturnes," to which Sosa says he listened every night for two years as a conservatory student in Cuba. Sendas by Omar Sosa �Caribbean Movement� and �Shirma� speak to Sosa�s rootedness in the lyrical, rhythmic, and harmonic heritage of the plantation islands where African and European cultures tragically entwined. In the violent forging of the world�s first truly modern people, social, cultural, linguistic, and musical displacements proved more flexible and accommodating than many of those same people, who shaped a contentious convergence of traditions into a changing same that persists into the unfolding present, ever yet to come. With expressive transcendence such as this, seeking to reduce the spiritual essence and inspiration of Sosa�s music to words is rather a fool�s errand. Better rather to listen, to contemplate, to perceive the pathway, to wander the sonic sendas coursing to the next way station without prejudice or preconception. To that end, Scott Price, Sosa�s longtime manager and friend relates, �We are using Sendas as the springboard for our first experiments in AI-generated Omar Sosa music videos.� Absent the opportunity to see and hear Sosa perform live, the palpable ideal, these ancillary audiovisual experiments further the ineffability of his artistic quest, the unique nature of the listening experience and all that ensues.

items._cn_summary: 这张专辑是古巴钢琴家Omar Sosa在2021年疫情期间于意大利Fazioli音乐厅的一次无脚本独奏即兴录音，后经混音加入人声片段、打击乐、循环、田野录音和收集的环境声响。作品源于他个人生活剧变与全球封锁背景下的偶然机遇，呈现出沉思而不断演化的艺术气质。Sosa拒绝风格标签，将爵士、拉丁、古典与实验声响融合，强调第一遍演奏的天然灵魂，并以“少即是多”为创作信条。专辑中既有对钢琴琴弦的直接拨弄与抚触，也有后期制作的细腻点缀，在空荡音乐厅的混响中构建出富有精神性和扎根感的声景。乐评引述Sosa关于人类精神迷失、传统与进化并行的观点，使整张专辑不仅是听觉实验，更承载着对灵性回归与音乐本质的思考。对于关注即兴、前卫爵士和跨文化融合的听众，这是一次兼具私密性与开放性的声音旅程。

items.body: Editor's note: When this set of recordings came to me, I was at a loss as to how to share it. It's not music, in any traditional sense (although there is some freestyle rapping), and a 'review' of such an artifact of reality seems superfluous to the content. Instead, I asked sound recordist Ian Brennan if I could simply use his own brief commentary and the recordings he made on the street in Chicago. Twenty-five people afflicted by gun violence participated, many from the very block we�d setup on. Many neighbors were pulled-in spontaneously. Almost every one in the community had been impacted by violence somehow� both on the receiving and the inflicting end, and many both. One woman had just come from a memorial service, another was on her way. That�s how far-reaching the violence. Almost no one went untouched. The Forgotten Parts by Chicago Gunfire Survivors By chance, we convened on the day that Trump ordered the deployment of the National Guard to the city. The recording took place on the front porch of the leader's ninety-four-year-old grandmother's house�right in the heart of the ��hood,� beneath the Midway Airport�s landing path. A pair of stray pitfalls stalked the block. But the grandmother warned not of gunshots, but the mosquitoes in her yard. The Forgotten Parts by Chicago Gunfire Survivors We were in a section of town that one man defined as �the forgotten parts.� Just a short jaunt from the designer clothes shops and posh hotels of the city�s Magnificent Mile, the Southside spawned such legendary Blues artists as Muddy Waters, Willie Dixon, and Howlin� Wolf. Jazz musicians like Lionel Hampton and even Benny Goodman, hailed from nearby. The Forgotten Parts by Chicago Gunfire Survivors The participants ranged in age from seventeen to sixty-seven, but the pattern held true. The person who�d asserted �you�ll really want to hear my story,� was the least compelling. The reluctant, the most moving. One elder�s tough facade broke down as she shared how she�d lost both her sons. She tearfully apologized, �I�m sorry. I�m sorry. I�m sorry.� But she had nothing to be sorry for. Society is the one that owes the apology� for the staggering statistical inequities of which no reasonable defense can be made. The Forgotten Parts by Chicago Gunfire Survivors Editor's note: The full set of recordings are available on Bandcamp. Any profits from this project will be donated to Cure Violence Global , who states that their mission is "advancing an evidence-based health approach to end violence globally." When I asked him about the background sounds, producer Ian Brennan added, "No music is added. It�s all sounds from the source environment. I also ran loops/drones on a different track in the background as they spoke, and when they ended up being incidentally/somewhat magically/eerily synchronous, that is what was used for a few pieces with 'accompaniment' like some of the rap freestyles."
items._genre: field recording / spoken word / sound art / experimental
items._cn_summary: 这张专辑是声音记录者Ian Brennan在芝加哥南区街头录制的环境声与幸存者口述，并非传统意义上的音乐作品。二十五位受枪击暴力影响的人参与了录音，其中许多人来自同一街区，年龄从十七岁到六十七岁不等。录音发生在一座九十四岁祖母家门廊前，背景包含飞机起降声、街区环境音与偶发的自由说唱。制作人明确表示没有添加任何音乐，全部素材来自现场。内容呈现了暴力阴影下普通人的脆弱与坚韧，一位失去两个儿子的老人反复道歉的场景尤为沉重。专辑以直接而克制的方式记录社区真实声响，将个人叙事与街头氛围融为一体，具有强烈的现实意义和文献价值，收益捐赠给反暴力组织Cure Violence Global。

items.body: SIRIUS is not a soundtrack that tries to justify its existence beyond the material it was originally created for. What Noah Rosa does is to open it up as a conversation with different artists. A cold wintry tone introduces the album. A glacial wind sweeps through. The score unfolds through slow transformations with harmony moving almost imperceptibly, but it is the dialogue between Habib El Bardi’s alto saxophone and Ruiqi Wang’s voice that gives the album its emotional centre. El Bardi’s saxophone drifts in and out of the texture with carefully judged restraint, while Wang’s voice functions as another timbral presence, dissolving into the surrounding electronics. Together they create music that feels suspended. That sense of openness is no accident. In the following interview, Noah Rosa explains that he gave both performers little more than a framework within which to improvise, allowing their own personalities to shape the music. One can hear that freedom throughout the score. Rather than sounding meticulously controlled, these pieces retain a quiet unpredictability, as though they are continually discovering themselves as they unfold. The second half of the album takes the project in a different, yet entirely coherent, direction. Rosa invited four artists to create what he calls “Refractions.” The title is more than a metaphor. These are not remixes but new perspectives on the same material, each revealing something that remained latent in the original. Vaiu’s contribution is perhaps the clearest example of this philosophy. Knowing her practice, centred on “the music underneath an instant” and on voice, time and technology as collaborators, makes perfect sense of her approach. She works from within the composition, drawing attention to tiny gestures, and the act of breathing itself. The refraction by Bios Contrast & Nilotpal Das is the album’s most transformative moment. His introduction of a quiet harmonium pulse reorganises the music from within, while fragments of the original score drift in and out of focus. Nothing feels imposed. Instead, the composition reveals another possible version of itself and, in the process, goes somewhere entirely different. Ioannis Nafpliotis pushes the material further towards electroacoustic abstraction, reducing much of the score to resonance, drone and silence, before Noah Rosa himself closes the cycle with his own “Refraction.” Rather than bringing everything full circle, Rosa acknowledges the creative dialogue established by the preceding reinterpretations. His own “Refraction” expands the sonic palette, making it more luminous and harmonically warmer. The collaborative spirit of the project extends beyond the “Refractions.” Habib El Bardi, Ruiqi Wang and the three artists behind the “Refractions” are not simply invited to decorate pre-existing compositions; they become co-authors of the record. That openness seems central to Rosa’s wider practice. Across The Radiant Tower, Drawing a Circle, The Two Headed Dragon of Forgiveness and now SIRIUS, he repeatedly returns to ideas of grief, transformation and renewal. As he explains, music is both his way of processing personal experience and of engaging with the world beyond himself. By the end, SIRIUS has become a conversation. To discuss further the production process for the album we spoke directly with Noah Rosa. Sirius began as a film score, but the album expands beyond the boundaries of the film through the four “Refraction” pieces. When you revisited the material after the film’s completion, what were you hoping to discover in the source recordings, and how did the soundtrack transform once it was allowed to exist as a standalone work rather than serving the image? Working on the score with the director Jean-Bastien was such a great experience and I really admired and connected with his vision for the film. Also getting to work with talented friends is such a gift so bringing on Habib and Ruiqi made the whole process feel special. After the film did its festival run I had gotten some good feedback on the music, it received a socan award, and I enjoyed listening to it, so we talked about putting out the soundtrack. I’d never done this before as I think of my composing work as pretty separate from my solo releases and also generally think that film music works best in the context it was created for. So with this in mind, I was more interested in re-approaching the music as a new entity and bringing new life to it. There was some music we made when initially building the sound language for the film that wasn’t used in the edit that I was excited to share. The film is really beautifully minimal and we wanted to pare back the music as much as possible to leave the stillness and quiet that it needed to hit right. So I did a new mix of all the cues to make them a bit more present for this release and during this process I thought it would be interesting to see how some other artists might respond to the material as I felt the raw elements from Habib and Ruiqi held a sort of integrity, and were imbued with the emotion of the film. I’m really grateful to evo-natura for supporting this project and Ioannis for contributing a track. I’ve always felt he understood what I was trying to do with both SIRIUS and my previous release Two Headed Dragon and I’m really happy to have it be the home for these works. Across releases such as The Radiant Tower, Drawing a Circle, The Two Headed Dragon of Forgiveness, and now Sirius, there seems to be a recurring interest in grief, transformation, spirituality, and the possibility of renewal. The Radiant Tower was conceived as a mourning album and “a eulogy to the old world,” while Drawing a Circle explored cycles of collapse and endurance, and The Two Headed Dragon of Forgiveness emerged from notions of suffering, forgiveness, and rebirth. Looking back across these works, do you see them as chapters of a larger artistic inquiry, or has each release represented a distinct attempt to process a particular moment in your life? Music is really my best language for processing what’s around me and further, my way to engage with the world. So both are true, all the works are personal and integrate processes I’m going through in my personal life but they also all hopefully work towards a greater truth beyond me. I’m very interested in transformation, change is often what we both want and fear the most… but it’s happening regardless. The album is shaped by collaboration at several levels: from Habib El Bardi’s alto saxophone and Ruiqi Wang’s voice in the original score to the contributions of artists such as Vaiu, Bios Contrast & Nilotpal Das, and Ioannis Nafpliotis in the “Refractions.” What were you looking for in these collaborators, and were there aspects of the material that surprised you when filtered through other artists’ sensibilities—particularly in the richly transformative “Refraction II” by Bios Contrast & Nilotpal Das? This is definitely one of the most collaborative projects I’ve released. Ruiqi and Habib are both incredible improvisers and I really only gave them scaffolding to work within. So much of their voice and personality comes through the music and I really think of it as a shared work. For the refractions I was interested in seeing how the raw elements could be completely recontextualized into these artists’ own sound worlds. I gave very little feedback or direction for them, mostly because these artists are all just incredible, but also because I wanted to be surprised by where they took it. Bios Contrast & Nilotpal Das is an artist I’ve admired for years. The way he’s able to move between long form minimalist drone and blown out idm with it making complete sense, the visual language, and sense of humour, all make him a really exciting artist. So I had no idea what to expect from the rework and loved how it brought this constant pulse from the harmonium while different layers from the score drift in and out. Similarly, when I first heard Vaiu’s track I was blown away by how she played in the musical landscape of the score but created something completely original, weaving her voice and sensibilities into the world. One striking aspect of your work is the way environmental sound, mythology, spirituality, and political reality coexist without ever feeling forced together. Both Drawing a Circle and Sirius direct their proceeds toward Palestinian causes, while albums such as The Two Headed Dragon of Forgiveness engage deeply with place, memory, and cultural exchange. What motivates your decision to connect these releases to concrete forms of solidarity, and do you see artistic practice as having a particular ethical responsibility in moments of ongoing crisis? I guess these are just reflections of what I care about, what I’m thinking about. I’m not making enough from music to live off anyways so I have a job to support myself. Proceeds from my releases could be supplementary to me or perhaps something a little more meaningful to someone else. It can feel a bit strange attaching monetary worth to art for me, so offering it as a gift in exchange for wealth redistribution feels more in balance. I believe all art making is political, and I hope my work carries some message of compassion and solidarity. It can also be quite a selfish and individualist thing to spend all your time trying to express your interior world so I think anything we can do to offset that by reconnecting with the world is important. Apart from artistic practice, I think we as humans all have a responsibility to reduce as much suffering as we can in our short times on this earth, or at the very least try not to add more. That is what ripples into eternity. Several of your releases—including Drawing a Circle and Sirius—have donated proceeds to Palestinian initiatives such as Grassroots Al-Quds and The Sameer Project. At a time when many artists feel pressure either to remain silent or to make overt political statements, how do you think about the relationship between sound, empathy, and action? Can ambient and experimental music contribute meaningfully to solidarity, even when it contains no explicit political message? If we are scared to even speak out about the greatest injustices happening in the world, the empires have already won. No career, status marker, or opportunity is worth turning a blind eye. I think the most important thing is patient everyday resistance and it requires constant attention. That being said I think we look to artists a little too much for their politics and social stance. Someone whose job it is to dream and play make believe might not always have the most grounded worldview. I really appreciate you asking these questions, even though I might not yet have the words to fully express what they mean to me. On a good day, I believe in music’s power to connect us with the ineffable and remind us that we are all manifestations of the same unity. Other days I think we might need less poetry and more direct action.. For now I’m just trying to be a decent person and stay connected to what matters. (Gianmarco Del Re)

items._cn_summary: 专辑以冬季冷冽的氛围开篇，将原声音乐转化为可对话的开放框架，邀请多位艺术家在即兴中共同塑造作品情感内核。中段以"Refractions"为名，邀请四组艺术家对原始素材进行再诠释——而非简单重混：有人聚焦于呼吸与微小的声音姿态，有人以手风琴脉冲重塑结构，有人推向电声抽象与寂静，最后由Noah Rosa本人以更明亮、更和声温暖的色彩收束整张专辑。这种协作模式模糊了作者与演奏者的边界，使每位参与者都成为共同作者，整张唱片在不同视角的折射中持续发现自身的多种可能。

items.body: To complement her interview in The Wire 511, Korean American composer Lucy Liyou creates an exclusive Wire mix Lucy Liyou grew up in Seattle, and as a child was a talented classical pianist. Her strengths, at first, were late Romantic and 20th century music; then she discovered the likes of Andrew Hill and Cecil Taylor, which inform the fiendishly difficult piano figures in her latest album Mr Cobra. Mr Cobra allowed Liyou to explore these influences, alongside her many others, including updated Korean folk opera, horror, vocality, narrative, maximalism, and families. This mix of Liyou's influences and inspirations was compiled exclusively for The Wire. Sharon Udoh “Great Is Thy Faithfulness” Cheryl E Leonard “moffen” Phew & Danielle de Picciotto “The Cat” more eaze “the producer” Blue Gene Tyranny “She Wore Red Shoes” Marran Gosov “Eifersucht” Borana Ramizi “Dying Is The Color Yellow” Iris Our “Splits and Wants” Lucy Liyou with Nick Zanca “Live in Paris February 2024” Samuel Beckett (performed by Billie Whitelaw) “Not I (1973)” Read Hugh Morris’s full interview with Lucy Liyou in The Wire 511. Pick up a copy in the online shop. Subscribers can read the full article in the digital archive here.
items._genre: experimental / contemporary classical / free jazz / folk opera / avant-garde
items._cn_summary: 韩裔美籍作曲家 Lucy Liyou 为 The Wire 独家策划的混音歌单，呈现其最新专辑《Mr Cobra》的多元影响谱系。她幼年研习古典钢琴，后受 Cecil Taylor 与 Andrew Hill 等自由爵士钢琴家的启发，发展出技巧艰深的钢琴语汇。歌单横跨多个领域：日本实验先驱 Phew 与 Danielle de Picciotto 的合作、加州作曲家 Cheryl E Leonard 的物件声响、印度尼西亚新晋音乐人 Iris Our 的作品，以及 Billie Whitelaw 朗读的 Samuel Beckett 名剧《Not I》。Liyou 的创作融合更新版韩国民间歌剧、恐怖美学、人声叙事与极大主义美学，将个人家族记忆与跨文化音乐传统编织为复杂的听觉文本。歌单作为访谈的延伸，揭示了她如何在钢琴这一传统媒介中注入前卫爵士的自由逻辑与当代实验音乐的解构精神。

items.body:
Old pals Christina Vantzou and Félicia Atkinson reflect on coastal living on their first collaborative album, blending environmental echoes from Rome, Normandy and Hydra with mellow synth, piano, Rhodes, vibraphone, lap steel, gongs and spoken word, pulling us into the sublime.

The third chapter in RVNG's ongoing "Reflections" series, 'Water Poems' crystallises a creative relationship that began way back in 2009. Vantzou and Atkinson have performed together before, most notably in 2019 at Philharmonie de Paris, but this is the first time the duo have made a record together. Both artists live by the sea, Atkinson in Normandy on the French coast, and Vantzou in Greece, using that shared experience to power a series of hazy dream sequences filled with subtle gestures. "The sea was not taken as a monolithic postcard," Atkinson explains. "But more of a person; an energy, a mystery, a complex character we face everyday, as human beings living by the sea."

Indeed, the esoteric energy of the sea - its tides, force, majesty and hypnotic, mystical pull, is captured by the duo's eddy of electroacoustic treatments and bespoke natural soundscapes. They recorded the material in a factory on the island of Hydra in Greece, at Villa Medici in Rome and at home in their respective studios, adding expressive environmental recordings from Delphi and the Eftalou Hot Springs. The record plays like a single, hazed thought, ebbing and flowing through the same shallow waters. Words emerge and disappear into carefully processed sounds at first, before forming sentences and whole thoughts on the second side. "How can a body swim," Atkinson mouthes. "How can a person dream?"

Gorgeously, quietly seductive gear from two of the very best at this sort of thing, one to file next to Meitei's sublime 'Sen'nyū (泉涌)' from last year - recline and drift into it.
items._cn_summary: 这张专辑是Christina Vantzou与Félicia Atkinson的首次合作录音，延续RVNG厂牌“Reflections”系列的第三篇章。两人长期居住在海边，作品以罗马、诺曼底、伊德拉岛等地的环境录音为基底，结合合成器、钢琴、电颤琴、滑棒吉他、锣与人声念白，构建出朦胧而流动的声音图景。素材录制于希腊伊德拉岛的工厂、罗马美第奇别墅及各自家中，并加入德尔斐和温泉的实地录音。音乐整体如同一段模糊的思绪，在浅水般的声场中起伏，文字起初隐没于处理过的声响中，随后逐渐浮现为语句与完整思考。乐评强调其捕捉了海洋作为复杂角色而非明信片式景观的隐秘能量，风格上与Meitei的《泉涌》相近，适合沉浸式聆听。

items.body:
On her third studio album, Brooklyn-based artist Frances Chang feels out the boundary between bedroom pop and lavishly orchestrated avant-experimentation, writing on a century-old grand piano and spiking her productions with jerky, unconventional electronic elements. The end result is somewhere between Aimee Mann and Cate Le Bon.

There's something unmistakably ramshackle about Chang's productions, but at the same time, it all sounds as if it's been meticulously planned. On opening track 'I can feel the waves', her voice never falters as it soars over casual phrases from her aging baby grand, but the it's the beats that immediately catch your attention, rupturing the calm with the momentum of a footwork demo. Chang's clearly an obsessive listener and it's this passion that lends her songs a breath of originality; they're classic in a sense, informed by Burt Bacharach, Chet Baker and Dionne Warwick, which actually makes sense. And where she takes the songs after they've been written is fascinating, building them out with instrumentation that's not exactly unexpected, it's just ever so slightly off-kilter. Those warbling strings on the ace 'Bad zen', or the buzzing micro-repetitions on 'Marry' - these sounds just nudge the material into a different zone and assert Chang's personality.

And as it develops, Chang's confidence grows. She's most successful when the guardrails are fully off - like on the brilliant 'No avatar'. Here, she latches her Robert Ashley-esque vocal lead to a wonky synth arpeggio that she follows with piano - or vice versa? The other instruments coolly fall into line: drums, bass and organ seem to flutter, flourish and fall at Chang's command, never quite going in the expected direction. Even advance single 'Auratones of Desire' makes more sense in context, its well-sculpted fusion of psych drum breaks, frittered farfisa organs and soft vocal affectations widening the album's reach considerably. Given it some time and attention for full reward.
items._cn_summary: 这张专辑在卧室流行的亲密感与前卫实验的繁复编排之间游走，创作基于一台百年老钢琴，却注入跳跃而不规则的电子声响。人声在松散随性的伴奏中保持稳定，节拍却以类似footwork的动能打破平静。弦乐颤音与细碎重复的电子音色让歌曲偏离常规，带出鲜明的个人印记。最突出的段落如《No avatar》中，近似Robert Ashley式的人声与歪斜的合成器琶音相互缠绕，鼓、贝斯和管风琴以出人意料的方式随之起伏。整体听感既有精心设计的痕迹，又保留一种临时拼凑般的松弛感，需要耐心聆听才能充分体会其层次与巧思。

items.body:
Barnt’s mnml 2012 kosmische waltzer for Matias Aguayo’s Cómeme is repackaged with a new master and Jens-Uwe Beyer + Crato revisions.

The kinky schaeffel is in effect on ‘gaffe’, which takes on a 2nd wind in its brighter, robust remaster, while Jens Uwe-Beyer evens out its irregularities for a disco-ready remix, and best of all, a ‘Magazine Hallucination’ mix that initially jettisons the beat and opens upwards, outward into majestic ambient zones, before its pulled back in a screwed echo of the original waltz groove.
items._cn_summary: Barnt 的《Geffen》原曲以轻巧歪斜的节奏与迷幻律动著称，此次再版经重新母带后更显明亮扎实，并收录 Jens-Uwe Beyer 与 Crato 的两首混音。Beyer 的版本将原曲的不规则感打磨得更为顺滑，偏向舞池适用；而 Crato 的“Magazine Hallucination”混音则先剥离节拍，向开阔的 ambient 区域延展，再以扭曲回响的方式拉回原曲的华尔兹律动，形成从氛围到律动的鲜明层次。整张单曲在 minimal 与 kosmische 传统中保持实验趣味，同时兼顾 remix 的多样性，适合偏好电子声响细节与空间感的听众。

items._cn_summary: 这张专辑以极简骨架般的节奏为核心，将后回响贝斯的克制、半拍电音、暗色车库与格科姆舞曲拧合在一起，带有粗粝的英国低音动能。各曲各有侧重：有的呈现棱角分明的断续格里姆律动，有的在高度压缩的半拍结构中融入类似佐姆比的旋律，有的偏向暗色车库的摇摆质感，有的则制造出变形的英国车库与格科姆混合体。整体在低音系统文化中保持实验性，声音处理简洁而锋利。

items.body:
The spirit of legendary film score composer Toru Takemitsu looms large over Kotaro Maruyama’s economical yet lush studies, ranging from sublime echoes of Japanese environmental ambient to beatific pulse poems edging on weightless Heinrich Mueller works.

"Composing primarily with the piano, Kotaro Maruyama creates music for a variety of visual media, including commercials and short films. Influenced by the composer Toru Takemitsu, he places importance on the “silence” and "ambience" of sound, aiming to create works where the music quietly depicts a scene.

Kotaro Maruyama's first solo album, "Vapor Curve," is constructed entirely from the sound source of the OP-Z digital synthesizer. Notably, he avoids the concept of harmony for a single tone, instead pursuing a unique "woven harmony" created by intricately layering multiple independent melodies. Using only the OP-Z, and recording everything in a single take without using a computer, Kotaro Maruyama's "Vapor Curve" is distinguished by its uncompromising production style. The minimalist melodies that are layered to create an ambient soundscape, along with the incidental noise that gives an organic texture to the inorganic electronic sound, showcase the raw appeal of sound that is imperfect."
items._cn_summary: 这张专辑以OP-Z数字合成器为唯一音源，全程不使用电脑，并以一次性录音完成，展现出高度限制下的创作巧思。音乐受武满彻影响，注重声音中的“沉默”与“氛围”，以多条独立旋律精密交织，形成独特的“编织和声”，而非传统意义上的和弦进行。极简的旋律层叠出广阔的环境音景，偶然的噪音为冰冷的电子声响注入有机质感，使作品在克制与丰饶之间取得平衡。整体上，它既延续了日本环境音乐的美学脉络，又以不完美的原始声音质感呈现了电子音乐的另一条路径。

items.body:
Influential Brum punks/post-punks Swell Maps captured in their snotty pomp, 1979, for the legendary John Peel Sessions - just a year before disbanding, and prompting everyone from Sonic Youth to Nirvana in their wake.

“Noisy, chaotic, and defiantly experimental, Swell Maps may not have found commercial success in their time, but their impact on music is undeniable. An inspiration to bands such as R.E.M., Sonic Youth, Dinosaur Jr., Pavement and Nirvana, with Kurt Cobain famously being a fan and often seen sporting a Swell Maps T-Shirt. A democracy within the confines of punk’s anything is possible, members Biggles Books, Jowe Head and brothers Nikki Sudden and Epic Soundtracks—helped shape the landscape of post-punk and DIY music. Now, for the first time in over 40 years, The John Peel Sessions brings together all three of their recordings for John Peel, a figure instrumental in championing their sound.

Formed in the early ’70s and fully realised by 1976, Swell Maps embodied the DIY ethos, launching their own label and self-releasing the jagged, frenetic debut single ‘Read About Seymour’ in 1978. Peel was an early supporter, playing their record as soon as it landed on his desk—a moment the band described as one of disbelief and elation. His regular airplay of their music helped solidify their cult status, and these sessions capture the raw energy, off-kilter melodies, and boundary-pushing creativity that defined them."
items._cn_summary: 这张合辑收录了Swell Maps于1979年为John Peel节目录制的全部三场录音，正值乐队解散前一年，保留了其粗粝、混乱且充满挑衅能量的现场状态。作为英国后朋克DIY场景的重要代表，他们自创厂牌并独立发行首支单曲，以锯齿般的吉他、偏离常规的旋律和即兴噪音构建出独特的声响。这些录音不仅展现了乐队在朋克框架内对实验性表达的追求，也解释了为何其影响能辐射至Sonic Youth、Nirvana等后来的独立与另类乐队。Peel的早期支持为乐队奠定了 cult 地位，而此次时隔四十余年的正式集结，让听众得以完整感受他们在录音室中未经修饰的原始爆发力。

items.body:
One of the UK’s most distinctive filmmakers returns to the sea, replete with his original synth score - as on ‘Bait’ and ‘Enys Men’ - but notably damper, deeply blue; surely evoking fellow Cornish native AFX’s ‘SAW II’, BoC interludes, Mordant Music, classic folk horror OSTs.

Centred around the tale of a trawler that returns, sans crew, to a Cornish harbour years after it was thought lost, ‘The Rose Of Nevada’ typically draws on what Mark Jenkin knows best - the people, places and metaphysics of the Atlantic peninsula - whilst ideally emphasising the atmosphere with his special ingredient score. His palette of tape-smudged analog synths feels especially washed out and suggestive of his subject in its briny tone and oceanic scale, which evidently works a treat as a discrete work in its own right, severed from imagery. 

There’s possibly a Kernewek word for “hiraeth”, or “sehnsucht” - a sense of longing, nostalgia - that we’re not aware of, but may perfectly fit the feeling of Jenkin’s music here. Sea-legged loops and sustained drones colour the air with a palpable melancholy in passage from the bittersweet tang of ‘Kneebone Barton’, as used on the trailer, and throughout the album’s patches of decaying wheeze, staining the surface like rust or efflorescence on weathered coves. 

And in the day-dreamiest sense it all fades in/out of consciousness with a perfectly ghostly wow and flutter, as leaching from ‘Through The Gaps’ parts into the slurred whorl of ‘What’s Your Name,’ ephemeral concrète of ‘Look At It’, and final folksy shuffle off into the horizon with ‘Rose of Nevada.’ Here’s looking forward to the film.
items._cn_summary: 这张原声专辑以磁带模糊的模拟合成器为核心，营造出潮湿、深蓝的海域氛围，与导演马克·詹金此前的《Bait》《Enys Men》一脉相承，但更显阴郁与怀旧。乐评指出其音乐让人联想到康沃尔同乡AFX的《SAW II》、BoC的间奏段落以及经典民间恐怖片配乐，在持续低音与摇晃循环中渗透出强烈的乡愁与失落感。作品脱离影像后依然成立，从《Kneebone Barton》的苦涩甜美到《Through The Gaps》的恍惚消融，再到结尾民谣式的渐行渐远，整体如潮汐般在意识边缘起伏。声音表面带有锈蚀与风化般的纹理，既私密又具有海洋尺度，是氛围电子与电影配乐思维的一次独特融合。

items.body:
Deep club modernist Sa Pa mints his own new label, Dub Techno For Life, with four top drawer cuts of textured, strident pressure tipped FFO classic Chain Reaction x Short Span.

Since 2015 Sa Pa has carved a heads-down path between techno, proper, and its conceptual adjuncts in ambient and sound designer atmospheres, most recently on Short Span and Astral Industries. Now taking matters into his own hands, the ‘Girls on Tour EP’ squares up his most robust club material alongside more experimental urges for a definitive self-portrait displaying a fine spectrum of strengths. 

The four tunes clearly speak to his diversity within a theme, checking for a firm touchstone in Andreas Tilliander aka Mokira with the 10 mins of rolling, claggy heft to ‘Mokira Ultra Dub’, unshelving his 2016 rework for deep ’26 ‘floors, alongside the puckered elegance of ‘Waiting For You’, harking to roots in Teutonic house minimalism, whereas the B-side attends to grubbier urges in the bittersweet, sludgy budge of ‘Modular System’, and lusher, abstract feels on the Actress or Rezzett-esque whorl of ‘World Saving Banger’.
items._genre: deep techno / dub techno / ambient / experimental
items._cn_summary: 这张EP是Sa Pa自创新厂牌Dub Techno For Life的首发，收录四首曲目，展现他在俱乐部声响与实验氛围之间的平衡。A面以《Mokira Ultra Dub》向Andreas Tilliander致敬，滚动厚重的低音与绵密质感延续Chain Reaction式经典dub techno脉络，《Waiting For You》则带有德国house极简主义的优雅。B面转向更粗粝的《Modular System》，在苦涩泥泞的律动中推进，而《World Saving Banger》呈现出类似Actress或Rezzett的抽象缠绕纹理。整体上，EP既呈现了Sa Pa最扎实的舞曲面向，也保留其声音设计与环境音乐的实验冲动，被视为一张具有个人总结性质的自我画像。

items.body:
Harking back to the vertiginous ambient sound of 2007's 'Language Barrier', Jeff McIlwain references Steve Reich and Susumu Yokota on his tenth album - his most cinematic, emotional project yet.

It makes sense somehow that after penning the poppy 'Long Light', McIlwain needed to walk in the opposite direction. Because the Lusine project has never just been one thing; since its beginnings in the late '90s, McIlwain has used the name to release choppy IDM, sturdy trip-hop, reductionist techno and placid ambient biz. Like 'Language Barrier', 'Melting Days' developed from film score work, and you can almost see the visuals on opener 'Sightline'. McIlwain uses the word "ambient" carefully; sure, the music is pegged to its washing, slow-motion pad sounds and submerged, brassy drones, but it's not entirely beatless. Here, McIlwain lets a molasses slow, almost inaudible kick do most of the heavy lifting, while a double-time click stands in for the hi-hat. On 'Bird's Eye', meanwhile, metallic hits flutter around the eroded central rhythm while McIlwain muffles his pads in the deep background.

He builds momentum on 'Pendulum' by waking up his deep, dubby soundscape with womping subs and wintery hits and on 'Intruder' curves the remnants of a voice around a skeletal, glitchy beat. McIlwain's idea of ambient music is open and all encompassing - it still belongs in the back room, but it's not just wallpaper.
items._cn_summary: 这张专辑回归了Lusine早期《Language Barrier》的环绕式氛围声响，同时延续了电影配乐式的创作路径。开篇曲目以缓慢铺展的合成器音垫和低沉的铜管嗡鸣构建空间感，几乎不可闻的慢速底鼓与双倍速点击声替代传统节奏骨架，形成介于有声与无声之间的律动。部分曲目在残响与碎拍中融入被切割的人声片段，或将金属质感的打击乐围绕磨损的节奏核心展开，而另一些则通过厚重的低音与冬季般清冷的音色推动情绪递进。整张专辑在氛围音乐与节拍音乐之间保持开放姿态，既适合置于背景聆听，又具备足够的细节层次供专注欣赏，体现了创作者对ambient概念的宽泛理解和个性化处理。

items.body:
Picking up where 2024's 'Trash Can Lamb' left off, Keith Freund blurs the line between acoustic instrumentation and DIY electronics on his latest full-length, unraveling his gentle, jazzy sessions with 8-bit beats and oddball FX.

Since the beginning, Freund has been fixated on the character of a sound rather than what that sound, on its own, might represent. His piano parts rarely come off as if they've been played by hand; after chopping them to shreds, he inevitably reconstitutes them into player-piano style impossible sequences, re-organizing the notes and re-sculpting the tone completely. On 'Over Sidewalk Bryum', for example, it's the piano that provides the track's rhythm, accented by radio interference and bit-crushed oscillations. And although Freund does less chipping at his horn parts, letting the sax soar over the chattering electronics, it's still subtly tweaked - nothing's ever quite what it seems.

A swamp of discarded blips and glitches help prop up 'I'll Find a Place for Us', and Freund's soft woodwind tones make their way through the noise initially - or at least that's what we're supposed to think. In time, Freund's sax emerges and the soft-hued, woodwind-like sound is revealed to be a red herring. But that's the kind of sleight of hand that Freund seems to revel in, creating glitchy, unstable music from soft, placid sound sources, not the harsh digital detritus you'd expect to find on a Mille Plateaux disc.
items._cn_summary: 这张专辑延续了前作的方向，将原声乐器与DIY电子设备之间的界限进一步模糊。钢琴部分经过切碎与重组，形成类似自动钢琴演奏的不可能序列，既承担节奏功能又被无线电干扰和位压缩振荡所修饰。萨克斯虽然保留了更多自然演奏感，在嘈杂电子声之上游走，但同样经过微妙处理，使听感始终处于似是而非的状态。开篇曲目以柔和的木管音色引入，随后揭示为声学假象，萨克斯真正浮现时，原本的温暖色调被颠覆。整体上，作品从平静的声音素材中构建出故障频出的不稳定结构，而非依赖生硬的数字残渣，体现出创作者对声音特质的持续关注和巧妙的错位手法。

Along with the likes of Total Freedom, Pineda’s work ushered the freshest wave of
items.body:
Club Romantico salute an unsung pioneer of modern club movements, Daniel Pineda ov Nguzunguzu - a producer of early Kelela and the short-lived Future Brown with Fatima Al-Qadiri - with a handful of lush yet venomous originals plus a Kelman Duran link-up 

You can’t talk about the 2010’s club sound without acknowledging Daniel Pineda’s influential, border-smudging productions as half of Nguzunguzu, with Asthma Maroof. Along with the likes of Total Freedom, Pineda’s work ushered the freshest wave of syncopated club music from the US at a time when Night Slugs (and Numbers.) and its American division, Fade To Mind, were hybridising UKF with Latin house, Jersey and B-More club and a groundswell of virulent Global South rhythms that began to percolate Westwards via blogs (this was the salient stuff when talking about blog-era, not the fidget-house pish) by the end of the ‘00s. 

Pineda’s ‘Landlocked’ firmly marks his return to a scene he sowed nearly decades ago, swerving from the heart-in-mouth pads and Dutch Bubblers-type groove to ‘De La Mama’, a a slower variant of that tresillo formula in ‘Gritos’, via the full-bore 145BPM intensity of ‘Fuerte’, a video clash-meets-Ballroom romp ‘Heavy Fact’, and the pneumatic subs and drill clack of a ‘Quema’ primed for carnival season. Another crucial bridge of Global South and Western club music, Kelman Duran tags in on the EP’s slowest, heaviest, ‘Loko 4 Eva’, strapped with below-belt quake and hardest drum cadence bound to get crowds slapping the walls.
items._genre: experimental club / electronic / global bass / deconstructed club
items._cn_summary: Daniel Pineda作为Nguzunguzu核心成员，曾深刻影响2010年代俱乐部音乐景观。这张EP标志着他重返舞池现场，以毒液般密集的声响与华丽合成器交织，横跨荷兰Bubbler律动、tresillo节奏变体、145BPM高强度节拍以及Ballroom式的冲击力，展现对全球南方节奏与西方俱乐部语法的娴熟嫁接。与Kelman Duran合作的曲目更以低音震颤与硬朗鼓组将氛围推向沉重边缘。整张作品既保留地下俱乐部文化的锋利棱角，又体现出制作人对声音层次的精密控制，是实验电子与舞曲传统之间的一次有力对话。

items.body:
Ezra Feinberg’s third album Soft Power sees the composer-guitarist enlist an impressive array of fellow musicians including Mary Lattimore, David Moore (Bing & Ruth), Jefre Cantu-Ledesma, and Robbie Lee.

"Defined by its abundance of melodies, repeating figures and ecstatic improvisations, Soft Power exudes an enlightened and transformative spirit to empower the listener. The compassionate, tender-hearted opener ‘Future Sand’ deftly interweaves flutes and steady arpeggios. The Reichian pulse beneath the soaring melody is played not on the customary analogue sequencer, but on finger-picked acoustic guitar, one of the lodestars of Feinberg’s compositional approach. ‘Soft Power’, the buoyant and mesmeric title track that follows builds over a rich bed of guitars and a reverb-y Rhodes melody reminiscent of a Strata East LP, its narrative arc bountiful in energy, optimism and future dreaming, a perfect accompaniment to long days of summertide.

‘Pose Beams’ blends the chamber-jazz approach of Penguin Café Orchestra with a balletic kosmische, climaxing with a galvanising crescendo and “free improv” section performed by fellow New Yorkers - Robbie Lee (piano) and Jefre Cantu-Ledesma, whose granular and modular synths sprinkle particle dust over the expressive drumming of John Thayer. ‘Flutter Intensity’ evokes in part the music of Cluster as played on acoustic guitars, which ping-pong across the stereo field, providing the canvas for a plaintive vibraphone line reminiscent of TNT-era Tortoise. Instruments move in tandem, but also drift and glide allowing them the space to hang in the air, the variegated rhythms, textures, and tones all laced into the fabric of the album.

At the centrefold of the albums 7-tracks is ‘The Big Clock’, a tryptic piece that evolves from pairs of stretched varying tones, creating fields of technicolour over an unabashed motorik beat, serving to offset the pastoral and ambient registers heard elsewhere. It features the first of two appearances from David Moore (Bing & Ruth) who plays lilting piano lines on the come-down. ‘There Was Somebody There’ returns to the album’s earlier wistfulness, a hard stereo-panned soundworld with lightly strummed, interlocking acoustic guitars combining to pigment a washy, painterly scene. David Moore and Jefre Cantu-Ledesma provide reviving synths, the underlying pulse that seems to simulate a life cycle; another day on Earth. The album closes with the reflective ‘Get Some Rest’ featuring Mary Lattimore, whose harp pluckings set a dreamlike tone against bare organic acoustics and flourishing flutes to create a sense of realignment and restoration.

Feinberg artfully transcends the listener to an enriched place, his compositions distinguished by the deep humanity that lies at their core, plugging the listener into a state of wide eyed being, open and alive. Soft Power then is Ezra’s own mantra but also one of power giving - a colourful catharsis translated into music. Feinberg’s music always speaks to the listener, but Soft Power, in whispering, speaks loudest."
items._genre: experimental / ambient / minimalism / kosmische / chamber jazz
items._cn_summary: Ezra Feinberg的第三张专辑《Soft Power》以原声吉他指弹脉冲为核心，融合大量重复旋律与即兴段落，邀请Mary Lattimore、David Moore、Jefre Cantu-Ledesma等乐手共同构建温暖而富有灵性的声响空间。开篇曲以长笛与稳定琶音交织，标题曲在吉他音床和混响电钢琴上铺陈出乐观的夏日叙事；后续曲目引入室内爵士、kosmische与自由即兴段落，钢琴、模块合成器与鼓点形成细腻对话。竖琴、原声吉他与合成器在立体声场中漂移、碰撞，既有Cluster式的极简肌理，也带Tortoise式的节奏质感。整张专辑在田园牧歌与motorik节拍之间切换，最终以竖琴与长笛的冥想性收束，营造出修复与重生的氛围，展现了作曲家对声响细节与情感流动的精准掌控。

items.body:
More slick sophisti-pop from the CPH scene via GB aka Gustav Berntsen, kinda heavily reminds us of a Japanoise/ jazz fusion take on Sam Prekop’s self-titled alltimer with bits of Red House Painters, Steely Dan and Prefab Sprout in there too.

Berntsen was stationed in London when he was writing 'Herzprung' and began to collect copies of the infamous free rag Metro, that he cut to shreds to fix up the lyrical portion of the songs. Once he had this in check, the Danish singer-songwriter called up his most trusted collaborators and booked a week at a studio "in the Swedish wilderness", where he dubbed the songs live to 24-track tape, encouraging improvisation and collaboration. And there's certainly a knottiness to this material that's unique to Bernsten; like many contemporary Copenhagen-based operatives, he's clearly well versed in classic rock and pop, from Fleetwood Mac and Steely Dan to Chick Corea and Haruomi Hosono, but he doesn't stop at pastiche, instead bringing his own absurdities to the table. "The Simpson's Season Six," he calls out harmoniously on opener 'Adrenaline', interrupting a stop-start drum fill and riffs that wouldn't sound out of place on a Gastr del Sol record. 

It would be hard to label 'Herzprung' post-rock, but there's a sense that Berntsen has at least learned from the genre's Chicago-era excesses. He seems to be driven by a holistic understanding of pop; at their heart, his songs are impeccably written, yet he's also not interested in taking the clearest path. On 'Belly', his cool-headed harmonies and almost tropicalia-strength choruses are complicated by winding instrumental sections and a phenomenally atmospheric dip into tape-fuckt cosmic ambience, while the lengthy 'Shit River' is a slowcore anthem that Berntsen expands with a full choir and an arsenal of synths.
items._genre: sophisti-pop / jazz fusion / experimental / slowcore / ambient
items._cn_summary: 丹麦唱作人在伦敦期间收集免费报纸《地铁报》，剪碎后重组为歌词，随后与固定合作者在瑞典野外的工作室用二十四轨磁带同期录音，鼓励即兴与集体改动。成品以旋律清晰的歌曲为骨架，但编曲不断偏离直线：开场曲穿插停走式鼓组与类似芝加哥后摇滚乐队的吉他动机，并混入人声喊话；另一首曲目在和声与近似热带流行副歌之外，转入磁带处理造成的宇宙氛围；较长的曲目则用合唱与合成器铺展。文章称其吸收爵士摇滚、经典流行与合成器流行等影响，但不止于模仿，带有个人化的荒诞感。

A quiet show of strength from Chicago’s budding and already highly sought after Dub Techno specialists, Kino Disk, hustling 11 exclusive permutations of dub-suffixed ambient, techno, and elemental abstraction by label regulars and new figures including Eustress, Infant, 8004 and many others, huge tip FFO Chain Reaction, Huerco S., Echospace, Short Span, Vialan.

In the space of 20 odd releases since 2024, Kino Disk has emerged as a key point of interest for off-grid dub aficionados. ‘American Dub Electronics’ now opens an ideal entry portal to their microcosm, rendering 11 exclusive bits that speak to the label’s fine grasp of variation within a theme. Trust it’s not wall-to-wall mark & moritz worship, rather a webbed spectra of interrelated, American POV’s on the same gauzy spirit from their collected vapours.

Building on the smouldering embers of over 30 years of precedents in this field, the set sways from the moonlit tidal movement of Psalm Star Electric’s ‘001’ to the unmoored slosh of 8006 (whose ‘8004’ was a sleeper gem of ’25) with a particularly nocturnal appeal. Eustress practices the most Catholic form of dub house in the darkly luminous ‘mm’, and Eden Aurelius’ Ring impress with the ASMR-like sensitivities of ‘Changeling’, and another label regular Point Survey with the phasing dub noise of ‘Print-Through’.

Keener observers may recognise those names already, but perhaps not the new ones here, notably Corbin Cary & Taylor White’s Permutia duo, secreting the fine lather chords and sandman bassline of ‘p1.2’, or HPIN with the early SND-style puckered glitch of ‘Remote’, Uos’ washed-out textures on Uos in ‘Uos Jelly’, and dreamily poised dub waltz of ‘Speedwalker’ by a.m.p & b.p.p.

items._cn_summary: 这张合辑收录芝加哥厂牌旗下及外围共十一首作品，以美国视角重构达布音乐传统，在氛围、科技舞曲与实验声响之间建立连续光谱。曲目从月光般潮汐流动的慢板氛围，到暗色发光的达布浩室，再到相位漂移的噪音和细碎故障音色，呈现同一主题下的多样变体；既有老面孔对类型语汇的娴熟运用，也有新组合带来的松散和弦与催眠低音。作为该厂牌自二〇二四年快速崛起后的理想入口，它展示了达布、氛围与电子交叉地带的当下美国样貌，并延续了三十余年相关脉络，适合关注地下电子与实验场景的听者。

items.body:
Showcasing contemporary Algerian sounds led by the gasba, a traditional reeded flute, 'My Heart is Dust Before Him' is a collaboration between Hive Mind and Oran's Édition Ahlem imprint.

In the Berber language, "gaspa" means "reed", and references the wind instrument that's central to some of the region's most gripping Bedouin folk and ceremonial music. On this 10-track anthology, Hive Mind plucks tracks from Édition Ahlem's recent catalogue; the label emerged in Oran from a record store and puts out cassettes since the early '90s. These selections are a little more contemporary and examine how the gasba forms have mutated and evolved in the last couple of decades, reacting to production changes while retaining the unique sound of the flute itself.

There's plenty to explore here, from the dimly lit distortions of Cheikh Tahar Oueld Marhoum's 'Naachak Fiha Ou Magoulhach' and Cheba Negouane's rai-adjacent 'Ychafouni Maghbounat' to Cheikh El Waal's woozy organ-led 'El Galb Maamar' and Mohamed Ain Larbaa's unexpectedly funky 'Sratli Khatra Kheleft L3ahed'.
items._cn_summary: 这张合辑聚焦阿尔及利亚当代gasba音乐，一种以传统芦苇笛为核心的贝都因民间与仪式音乐形式。Hive Mind与奥兰的Édition Ahlem厂牌合作，从后者近年的磁带目录中精选十首曲目，展示gasba在近二十年中如何随制作技术变迁而演化。选曲涵盖昏暗失真的声响、接近rai风格的编排、管风琴主导的迷幻段落以及出人意料的放克律动，在保留笛声独特质感的同时融入当代录音美学。厂牌本身从唱片店起家、自90年代初持续发行磁带，具有鲜明的独立与地下色彩，为这些传统音色提供了更具实验性的呈现语境。

items.body:
Necessary reissue of Marc Leclair’s immaculate Y2K micro-house/dub-house 12” as Akufen, dispensed by Low End Activist’s guess-again BRUK sibling to Sneaker Social Club - huge RIYL Maurizio, Studio 1, Mike Huckaby.

‘Architextures 1 -2 -3’ is a sought-after slice of hypnotic house by a noted pioneer of the micro-house movement that emerged in the late ‘90s. Its reissue arrives in the wake of a re-up for Marc Leclair’s (aka Akufen) sole solo album ‘Musique Pour 3 Femmes Enceintes’ (2005) with a strong reminder of his pivotal role in dressing house music down to fundamentals around the millennium, as deployed in Richie Hawtin mixes and praised for its exquisitely efficient, effortless, hiccuping funk.

It’s really all about the  A-side’s ‘Architexture 1’, a pendulous 127BPM roller inflected with chef’s kiss dub chords and frisky drums, on one of the smoothest, deepest basslines since ‘M5’. There’s a good reason why it’s been fetching triple figures on 2nd hand markets, so BRUK are doing the Lord’s work with this reissue, which also includes the slower, sub-heavier swivel of its Pt. 2, and more signature, strutting clip of his tight sampling tekkerz on Pt. 3.

TIP!
items._cn_summary: 这张再版12寸收录了Akufen在千禧年前后开创micro-house风格的三个代表曲目。A面曲目以127BPM的律动为核心，融合dub和弦与细密鼓点，贝斯线深邃平滑，被乐评视为该风格中接近Maurizio经典质感的作品。第二首放慢速度并加重低频，呈现更摇摆的dub-house面向；第三首则展现其标志性的密集采样剪辑技术。乐评指出，这张唱片在二手市场长期高价流通，此次再版让更多听众得以接触这位micro-house先驱的关键创作，并强调了他在Richie Hawtin混音中的重要作用，以及他对将house音乐剥离至基本元素的历史贡献。

items._cn_summary: 这张专辑是利兹大编制乐队在灵性爵士路线上的第三作，与前作注重悦耳旋律不同，重心转向即兴演奏。乐评指出，作品通过拍子错位和静与动的强烈对比营造紧张氛围，在混沌的独奏交替中突然凝聚为整齐的合奏，复杂复合节奏的推进也带来兴奋感。整体呈现了自由即兴与精密编排之间的张力。专辑延续了乐队擅长的灵性爵士方向，但更强调现场演奏的不可预测性。乐评特别提到，段落间的动态落差和节奏错位制造出悬而未决的张力，而即兴独奏的混乱中会骤然出现整齐的集体爆发，复杂复合节奏层层加速，形成强烈的听觉冲击。对于关注自由即兴、前卫爵士和节奏实验的听众，这张作品提供了值得研究的声响组织方式。

items.body: Rather than relying on brute force, Beatrice M. favors restraint, allowing space, texture and movement to do the heavy lifting. The result is a sophisticated, deeply atmospheric debut that confirms her as a compelling new voice within Bristol’s ever-evolving bass continuum. Drawing from dub, bass music and sound-system culture Beatrice M. makes an assured full-length debut with Sinking on Bristol’s Tectonic Recordings, with label head Pinch lending engineering expertise that keeps every detail razor-sharp. Across eleven tracks, the album balances tenderness and tension, drawing from dub, bass music and sound-system culture without ever feeling confined by genre. Atmospherics do much of the storytelling, as shimmering hi-hats, cavernous low-end and richly textured synths create spaces that feel both intimate and immense. By the time “Motion” arrives, the album fully reveals its rhythmic confidence, where crisp percussion and fluid basslines evoke a meeting point between Bristol’s dub heritage and contemporary European club music.​ “Juice,” featuring Sir Hiss, channels echoes of Basic Channel while pushing into smoked-out, dancefloor-ready territory through weighty 4/4 momentum and meticulous dub production. Meanwhile, “Help” stands among the highlights, pairing fractured breaks, rolling bass and spoken-word reflections on everyday urban life to ground the record’s immersive sound design in human experience. Throughout Sinking, the production remains immaculate, the arrangements economical and every element purposefully placed. Rather than relying on brute force, Beatrice M. favors restraint, allowing space, texture and movement to do the heavy lifting. The result is a sophisticated, deeply atmospheric debut that confirms her as a compelling new voice within Bristol’s ever-evolving bass continuum. Sinking is available on Tectonic. [Bandcamp] Sinking by Beatrice M.The post Beatrice M. :: Sinking (Tectonic) first appeared on Igloo Magazine.
items._cn_summary: Beatrice M.的首张专辑《Sinking》以克制与空间感为核心，在dub、bass music和音响系统文化的交汇中展开。制作由Tectonic厂牌主理人Pinch把控，细节清晰锐利，编排经济且每个元素都经过精心布置。闪烁的hi-hats、深邃的低频与富有质感的合成器共同构建出既私密又宏大的声场。曲目《Motion》以清脆打击乐和流动贝斯线展现布里斯托dub传统与当代欧洲俱乐部音乐的融合；《Juice》与Sir Hiss合作，在厚重4/4律动中透出Basic Channel式回声；《Help》则通过破碎节拍、滚动贝斯和关于城市生活的口语念白，将沉浸式声音设计拉回日常经验。整张专辑在温柔与张力之间保持平衡，不依赖蛮力，而是让空间、纹理和运动本身承担叙事，呈现出一部成熟而富有氛围感的电子低音作品。

items.body: Re: Echo Mist Light offers a spellbinding collection of re-imagined pieces based on the initial album by Wahn. This release celebrates the 500th release of the independent imprint, a well-known publisher which cannot be missed by avid followers of adventurous and multifaceted forms of electronic music. Abstract motifs meet swelling tones Re: Echo Mist Light by Wahn   Wahn (alias Erwan Charier) is a highly acclaimed project from France, with roots in a plural field of electronic subgenres, from dubby ambient to challenging IDM with a dream feel, glitch, and shifting techno-ish moods. His last album, recently published on Mahorka, introduces the listener to an intriguing, enigmatic, and shadowy mental landscaping journey through kinetic hypno-grooves, swelling digital ambiences, and cinematic atmospherics. It progressively installs a profound sonic bath where abstract motifs meet swelling tones and sometimes crystal-like detached melodies. We can easily appreciate the amount of ideas developed in the album and the thoughtfully crafted soundscapes brought up to the fore. Re: Echo Mist Light offers a spellbinding collection of re-imagined pieces based on the initial album by Wahn. This release celebrates the 500th release of the independent imprint, a well-known publisher which cannot be missed by avid followers of adventurous and multifaceted forms of electronic music, at the frontier between radical avant-garde and more immediate, transportive soundscapes. For this special album, the label reunites a bunch of sound artists from its family circle. Musically, this re-work oscillates between vaporous downtempo feel (notably with Signalstoerung), post-industrial mechanized, fractal-like glitchy ambiences (Brainquake, Valance Drakes), almost groovy trip-hop excursions (Mas&Delayer), and abstract minimalism covered by impressionist, soothing synthadelic waves (Dissolved). The album closes with the two most expressive and emotionally inclined lysergic ambient tracks of the album, designed by Cognition Delay, then Substak. Despite its diversity and wider stylistic inclination, the album keeps the spirit of the original Wahn’s album and contributes to positioning the Mahorka label among key representatives of electronic-based music with a fancy for broader experimentations and a larger vision about what sonic worlds mean. Quite recommended for fans of thrilling ambient dub, downtempo, and neo-psychedelic purposes. Re: Echo Mist Light is available on Mahorka. items._cn_summary: 这张专辑是对Wahn原作的重新构想合集，由Mahorka厂牌为纪念第500张发行而策划，集结多位声音艺术家参与。作品在朦胧的缓拍氛围、后工业机械化故障声响、近乎律动的神游舞曲以及抽象极简主义之间游走，结尾两首由Cognition Delay和Substak创作的曲目呈现出更具情感表达的迷幻氛围。整体上，专辑保留了原作的幽暗与催眠特质，同时通过不同艺术家的处理拓展了风格边界，使数字环境声场与具象旋律片段交织，形成深沉而富有层次的声音景观。对于关注实验电子、氛围缓拍和新迷幻方向的听众，这张作品提供了丰富的聆听维度。

The Czech-Slovak trio of experimental musicians apparently share Pete Kember and Jason Pierce’s guiding principle of “taking drugs to make music to take drugs to”. The group’s psychedelia was inherited from the freewheeling 1960s, a decade when Western music – from rock to minimalism – was infused with the meditative transcendence of sustained tones. But the most important question is left unanswered: what drugs to take to make drone music to take drugs to? The album’s title may offer some cues. Born... items.body: Review by Fercandio46 — Immersing themselves in an aesthetic that is as surreal as it is claustrophobic, the Norwegian quartet employs various elements, electronica, space rock, and psychedelia, yet does so in a way that sounds both modern and vintage; specifically, a vintage quality reminiscent of the 1920s and the silent film era, a time defined by a distinct, fully developed, and mature artistic language. The instrumentation features two guitars and drums, alongside Mellotron, piano, and keyboards."Colours Out of Space," the opening track, rises like a multi-layered wall of sound, combining rock with a dark, aggressive brand of electronica that sets the stage for vocals that are as progressive as they are prophetic. There is a guest cello as well as a French horn; and just as "Colours Out of Space" is a concept album dedicated to the work of H.P. Lovecraft, "Leng Plateau" opens with an ominous post-rock sound that spreads and permeates the atmosphere, while percussion, resembling the sound of clashing crystals, draws us into its world.CosmiK is infectious, it leaves its mark; were it a blank screen, it would turn black. Its rhythm gets under your skin, skillfully balancing rock and electronic elements, with traces of Krautrock revealing themselves upon a second listen, further enriching the album.Its greatest achievement is recapturing that lost magic, a blend of palmistry and spiritual essences that, by the time "Hutchinson Cipher" arrives, becomes something analog, tactile, and visceral. The sheer force of the instruments demands a physical connection, a possession of the body, to experience and inhabit a dimension that feels far more grounded in the earthly realm.Whether the intensity ramps up or dials back, the hypnotic atmosphere never breaks; instead, it fosters a kind of trance, a voluntary immersion in an illusory fantasy. With the arrival of "Strange Days," the music pauses for a breath, featuring a piano accompanied by wind-like echoes... followed by a choral section reminiscent of Popol Vuh. After all, aggression and violence may promise intensity, but they don't preclude fine songwriting, as is clearly the case here. The experience feels all too brief, likely because it is so enjoyable; listening to Pixie Ninja and Colours Out of Space is like watching a film that leaves you wanting more, even though it seems to hail from an era before sequels existed.

items.body: Review by arymenezes — Progarchives is my primary source of information, and this album was one of the excellent discoveries I made here.It begins with incredible keyboard phrasing. The drums add many inventive layers to the harmonies. At the minute-and-a-half mark, there are some passages reminiscent of ELP, featuring combinations of different keyboards. They manage to keep the energy high-voltage throughout its entire length.The piano on the second track is vibrant, and the drum rhythms create a smoothy contemplative swing feel. Overall, the result is reminiscent of cabaret music mixed with blues-rock. It is a very short track featuring vocals, whereas the preceding track is instrumental.Their compositional skills are truly highlighted on this music, as they seek out very organic and fluid harmonies. The arrangements are also quite interesting, as the role of the bass is more clearly defined, this time, through the keyboards and bass drums. The drum turnovers always reveal new subtleties when executed.Another track featuring vocals, which are always in english. For now, the style leans more towards rock, with a pronounced drum beat. Instead of traditional guitar solos, the solo sections are performed on the only two instruments used.The blues returns on the 5th track, taking on a slightly danceable feel. It isn't a masterpiece of creativity or diversity, but it certainly gets the job done.The sixth track sticks with some beautiful blues but employs arrangements and tones quite different from those used previously. They excel at knowing how to highlight the most inspired instrument ? in this case, the keyboards ? through the mix and editing. Even the drum fills have a bluesy atmosphere. It's a short track.The organ opening of the next track is enchanting, increasing the atmosphere with a more spiritual quality. After nearly a minute and a half of this, the rest of the instruments and the vocals enter respectfully. The unhurried tempo maintains a sense of reverence and transcendence. The composition concludes with the organ ? an emotive finish that layers sounds with clarity and consistency. It is no coincidence that this is the album's longest track, 'cause it's one of the most inspired.The vocals are (effectively) sustained on the eighth track. The cadence remains on the slower side. In a way, it is like hearing a second take on the musical concept explored in the previous track. The organ's timbre is truly wonderful.The next track is a magnificent adaptation of Ravel's 'Bolero' with a kraut flavor. It is intense, like the original composition, with the added advantage of being a condensed version.A more melodic approach prevails on the 10th track. Once again, the pairing of piano and organ creates a fabulous, ethereal combination. It is a shame the sound is a bit muffled.The final track on the LP is pure Krautrock. Electronic harmonies blend together with great freedom. The drums are situated that feel halfway between a march and a loop; to my ears, a great tune.My edition of the CD is the latest British pressing. It includes two bonus tracks, originally released as the band's only single (released on the same year of the album). The first music is reminiscent of early Pink Floyd psychedelia ? lighthearted, unpretentious, and breezy. The second track leans more towards The Moody Blues and Procol Harum vein; even the vocal style takes on a somewhat syrupy quality.General view of the CD: their technique isn't outstanding, and they lack a bit of variety on the instrumentation (however, they couldn't go so far on this matter, with only two members twogether). Their compositional habilities are exceptional, the arrangements are high-skilled, as well as most of the timbres.Rating: 4.1 of 5 stars.

items._cn_summary: 这张专辑以键盘为核心，开篇即展现密集的键盘乐句与多层次的鼓击，和声编排带有ELP式前卫摇滚印记。钢琴与管风琴交替主导，布鲁斯与卡巴莱元素融入摇滚框架，低音线条通过键盘与低音鼓清晰呈现。人声曲目较少，英文演唱，节奏偏慢，管风琴段落营造出接近宗教性的氛围。后半部分将拉威尔《波莱罗》压缩改编为具有德国泡菜摇滚质感的版本，电子和声与进行曲/循环式鼓点结合。整体上，作品在布鲁斯摇滚与前卫实验之间保持平衡，编曲注重有机流动的声部关系，鼓的转换和键盘音色处理是亮点。

items.body: Review by Fercandio46 — A trio with an aesthetic as steadfast as it is static might well have found itself feeling hemmed in at times; it is no coincidence that Les Claypool has formed various side projects, from Sausage in 1994 and Oysterhead in 2000, through the different "Colonel Claypool" incarnations, to his most recent venture, the Claypool Lennon Delirium.And yet, a band as endogamous as Primus had switched drummers for Brown Album, bringing in Bryan "Brain" Mantia, and featured that strange machinery seemingly drawn from German Expressionism; it is no coincidence that, whenever the music veered into progressive territory, it employed techniques characteristic of Krautrock.After a seemingly live introduction, the album truly kicks off with "Fisticuff," where the bass and drums take divergent paths and Larry LaLonde does what he does best: creating atmospheres and psychedelic backdrops, sometimes subterranean, other times soaring, until "Golden Boy" propels us onto an unstoppable funk-rock bus. That track became a live staple for the band from then on; noteworthy here are LaLonde's dexterity, he seems to have grown increasingly fluid, and the magic of Primus, a band that sounds different even while sounding the same... because they present the illusion of repetition."Over the Falls" stands out for many reasons: it has an acoustic sound featuring the double bass, it is dark, and... it is a song. It follows a song structure, yet it sounds so experimental in its apparent simplicity.The machinery was firing on all cylinders on "Shake Hands With Beef", allowing one to hear the track as a whole or deconstruct it part by part, and Lalonde's solo here leans toward jazz-rock. Just as "Camelback Cinema" is a blast of metal-tinged rock, "Hats Off" is one of those playful tracks that nonetheless doesn't shy away from constant rhythm shifts. The psychedelic, yodeling funk of "Puddin' Taine", played at a frenetic pace, leads into one of the album's gems, "Bob's Party Time Lounge" (which lasts four and a half minutes in the studio version, and seven and a half in the live version on the Rhynoplasty EP)the track plays masterfully with space, highlighting the bass and the song's abrupt breaks to create a dramatic tension that makes it irresistible."Duchess and the Proverbial Mind Spread" seems to flirt with reggae, in its own unique way, while "Restin' Bones," featuring Led Zeppelin-esque drumming and spoken-word vocals from Lalonde and Claypool, hints at the melodies of a more contemporary Tom Waits."Coddingtown" returns to the band's punk roots, showcasing virtuoso bass work throughout, before leading into "Kalamazoo," where the album picks up the pace with highly experimental guitar and bass, a catchy melody, and a full array of musical elements, including the use of chromaticism.A highlight of "The Chastising of Renegade" is when Lalonde takes the reins; his solo evokes everyone from Robert Fripp to Tony Iommi. Arnie closes the album with a compelling, suspended atmosphere, featuring Zeppelin-esque drums, fretless bass, and fuzz guitar, while Les recites the lyrics.A good album, featuring their signature sound alongside new elements, though one has to scratch the surface to find them, like panning for gold among river stones (an image Claypool is fond of) yet it feels like a bridge between Tales From The Punchbowl and Antipop. Still, gold always shines the same.

items._cn_summary: 这张专辑是Primus更换鼓手后的一次风格聚合，贝斯与鼓常走不同路径，吉他手Lalonde以氛围化演奏构建迷幻底色。作品在放克摇滚骨架中融入Krautrock式机械律动、爵士摇滚独奏、金属段落、雷鬼节拍与暗黑民谣色彩。原声低音提琴、口语化人声、频繁变速与骤停结构制造出戏剧张力。部分曲目既有朋克式的直接冲击，也有接近前卫摇滚的复杂编排；吉他独奏跨越Fripp到Iommi的谱系。整张专辑在看似重复的声响中呈现细微变化，适合逐层拆解聆听。
